10751-oregon-washington-and-alaska-sight:
E. L. Lomax, general passenger agent of the Union Pacific System, issued Oregon, Washington and Alaska: Sights and Scenes for the Tourist in 1890. The guide, offered by the railway's passenger department at Omaha, lists agents from Albany to Boston and points travelers toward the Pacific Northwest and Alaska. Illustrations show the lands the trains served.

The book mixes practical travel help with praise for scenery, towns, and routes. It captures the booster spirit of western railways, eager to fill their cars with tourists. Modern readers get a period guide to the Northwest, and a record of how railroads sold the West.
10958-an-unwilling-maid-being-the-histor:
Jeanie Gould Lincoln set this 1897 romance in Connecticut and New York during the American Revolution. Betty Yorke, born Wolcott, is a spirited young woman whose loyalties are tested by war, family, and love. Chapters follow her through bullets for defence, a prisoner named Oliver, a journey inside British lines, and the De Lancey ball, where love and loyalty pull opposite ways.

Betty's maid Moppet, a knot of rose-coloured ribbon, and a face on the wall add mystery and humour to the plot. Lincoln writes for young readers, keeping the history light but present: Whigs and Tories, couriers, and divided towns. The novel charms through Betty herself, unwilling at first, brave when it counts, and loyal to her own heart.
12667-travels-of-richard-and-john-lander:
Robert Huish compiled this 1836 account from the papers of Richard and John Lander, who sought the course and end of the River Niger. It opens with a survey of earlier African travellers, including Park, Denham, and Clapperton, before following the Landers inland. Markets, rulers, deserts, and river towns fill the long road south.

The narrative stresses hardship as much as discovery: heat, hunger, hostile bands, and long waits for guides and safe passage. Huish frames the journey as a key step in mapping West Africa for British readers. The book remains a full, first-hand record of exploration before steam and rail changed the continent.
1310-the-annals-of-the-parish-or-the-chr:
John Galt tells, year by year, the chronicle of Dalmailing, a Scottish parish, through the voice of its minister, Micah Balwhidder. From 1760 to 1809 the parish changes: mills rise, roads come, wars take sons, and old customs fade, all noted with a minister's dry humor.

Galt writes Scots life with warmth and realism, and the annals form a social history in miniature. The book made his name and founded the Scottish parish tale. It suits readers who like quiet chronicles and the texture of a community changing. Galt's parish chronicle gives a whole community's change in miniature.
13183-in-the-days-of-chivalry-a-tale-of-:
Evelyn Everett-Green's tale of the Black Prince's time opens in the warm autumn of Gascony, where forests turn russet, scarlet, and gold. Twin eaglets are the book's young heroes. They grow up among knights, priests, and woodmen. Chapters run from Father Anselm to the King, the Prince, and the war path. Everett-Green writes for young readers who love romance and history.

Later pages debate free will, with one speaker denying that God binds men's wills or makes them blind agents. An old man steeped in Moorish lore is blamed for gaining mastery over minds, not by demons but by wicked will. Joan Vavasour, kind and firm, promises care for an old servant's wife. The tale mixes chivalry, faith, and adventure in the old style.
13485-an-enquiry-concerning-the-principl:
Frances Reynolds asks in 1785 where our ideas of beauty come from, and what taste, grace, and genius share. Her enquiry, reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society with an introduction by James L. Clifford, argues that grace in the object, genius in making it, and taste in perceiving it are one quality seen from three sides.

Grace, she says, rests more on mental than bodily beauty, and sits between sublimity, which no rules can teach, and lower pleasures. Flowers please, she suggests, when they resemble a pre-formed idea of beauty in the human species, even when the mind cannot name the cause. Reynolds writes as a woman thinker of her age, plain, careful, and eager to ground feeling in reason.
13531-amos-kilbright-his-adscititious-ex:
Frank R. Stockton's 1888 collection opens with Amos Kilbright and his adscititious experiences, told by Richard Colesworthy, a practical attorney in an eastern town. Colesworthy, little given to speculative theory outside his profession, lends weight to a strange tale of a man acted upon by unseen powers.

Other stories follow: The Reversible Landscape, Dusky Philosophy in two expositions, and Plain Fishing. One exposition tells of seven devils, with Brother Peter closing his Bible with a bang though he cannot read a word of it. He preaches that women, possessed sevenfold, should submit to male direction. Stockton mixes fantasy, satire, and dry American humour throughout.
13887-dr-allinson-s-cookery-book-compris:
T. R. Allinson published Dr. Allinson's Cookery Book in 1915 as a guide to vegetarian cooking. A long index lists dishes from almond cheesecakes and apple charlotte to orange mould and pancake pudding. A month's menu for one person helps beginners plan meals. Allinson, a doctor, links food with health throughout.

Recipes avoid meat and stress simple, wholesome ingredients. Apple cookery gets many entries, from dumplings and fool to fritters and sauce. Soups, puddings, and savoury dishes follow in alphabetical order. The book reflects Edwardian interest in diet reform. It still serves cooks who want plain, meat-free Victorian and Edwardian recipes.
14004-the-every-day-life-of-abraham-linc:
Francis Fisher Browne built this life of Abraham Lincoln from the memories of men and women who had known him face to face. Published after years of planning, it favors daily scenes over grand state papers. Courtrooms, campaign trails, small-town streets, and White House rooms all appear in turn. Lincoln emerges as a neighbor first and a president second.

Anecdotes carry the argument. Friends recall his humor, his patience with callers, and his plain talk on the stump in southern Illinois, where armed crowds sometimes threatened him. Later chapters follow his wartime leadership, his pleas to the border states, and his care for popular government under strain. Readers looking for Lincoln the man, rather than Lincoln the monument, will find him here in the voices of his own circle.
14824-furnishing-the-home-of-good-taste-:
Lucy Abbot Throop's 1920 book, revised from earlier editions, sketches period styles in interior decoration and suggests how to use them in homes of today. Egypt and Greece open the survey, followed by the Renaissance in Italy and the development of decoration in France.

Louis the Fourteenth, the Regency and Louis the Fifteenth come first, then Louis the Sixteenth and the Empire. English furniture follows, from Gothic days to Queen Anne, Chippendale, Robert Adam, Hepplewhite and Sheraton. Pictures of panel spacing, pilasters and cornices show principles that fit large and small houses. Throop writes for readers who want taste with history behind it.
16019-phelim-otoole-s-courtship-and-othe:
William Carleton's Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry supplies five tales in this volume, led by Phelim O'Toole's Courtship. Phelim, an only son, inherits a snug half acre won by his grandfather Tyrrell. Tyrrell earned it with his reaping hook. A harvest trip to England brought home eight guineas, a new hat, and a staff. The family ground at Teernarogarah sets the scene.

Wildgoose Lodge, Tubber Derg or The Red Well, Neal Malone, and Art Maguire or The Broken Pledge fill out the book with courtship, crime, drink, and broken promises. Carleton's peasants talk, joke, and quarrel in lively dialect, and his stories mix comedy with moral judgment. The volume is a strong entry point to his Irish world.
16396-a-conspiracy-of-the-carbonari:
Louise Muhlbach's Conspiracy of the Carbonari, translated by Mary J. Safford and published in New York by F. Tennyson Neely in 1896, opens after Esslingen. It was the evening of May 22, 1809, a day inscribed in blood-stained letters. It brought Napoleon his first dimming of fortune. Germany, especially Austria, saw a first ray of dawn after a long, gloomy night. Tilsit, Austerlitz, and Jena had humiliated Germany, while Erfurt marked Napoleon's triumph.

From that turning point grows a tale of secret societies, patriots, and plotters working against French power. Muhlbach, author of Berlin and Sans-Souci and Frederick the Great, writes popular historical romance with sweep and feeling. Readers who like Napoleonic intrigue will enjoy this dramatic novel.
16958-the-cross-and-the-shamrock-or-how-:
An 1853 Boston tale by a missionary priest, writing under a pen name later known as Hugh Quigley, speaks straight to Irish Catholic workers in the United States. The O'Clery family faces death, the poorhouse, hard bosses, and smooth tempters, and the book tracks their trials, falls, and returns to faith. Mass in a shanty and scenes of prayer anchor the plot.

Meant both to entertain and to teach, the novel defends Catholic belief against scoff and pressure in a new land. Its long, plain chapters mix home drama with points of doctrine for servant readers. Today it reads as a vivid record of Irish immigrant life, faith, and pride in the young republic.
1831-the-lock-and-key-library-classic-my:
Julian Hawthorne edits another Lock and Key volume, this time of classic mystery and detective stories, gathering tales that defined the form. Famous names and forgotten writers share the pages. Hawthorne's classic volume gathers tales that had already proved their staying power.

The collection traces mystery from ghostly tales to logical detection, showing how the genre grew. For readers building a shelf of classic crime, this volume offers a broad, well-chosen survey. Ghost stories beside detective puzzles show mystery's two roots, fear and reason. A reader new to classic crime could start here and find the whole field.
18709-the-best-short-stories-of-1921-and:
Edward J. O'Brien edited this yearly volume at Boston with Small, Maynard and Company, after six prior years of best story picks. It gathers the best American short stories of 1921 from magazines such as the Century, the Dial, Harper's, Scribner's, and the Saturday Evening Post, with a yearbook of the American short story. Authors range from Sherwood Anderson and Ellen Glasgow to Susan Glaspell, Fannie Hurst, and Wilbur Daniel Steele.

O'Brien thanks editors and publishers for leave to reprint, and invites readers' corrections and tips. The book closes with copyright pages spanning 1920 to 1922. It serves as a snapshot of American short fiction in a single year.
19002-alice-s-adventures-under-ground-be:
Lewis Carroll published this facsimile in London and New York in 1886, reproducing the original manuscript book he had made by hand, later developed into Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. The volume carries thirty-seven illustrations by the author himself and was priced at four shillings. Its chapters follow the familiar shape in shorter form.

Alice falls down the rabbit-hole and swims in a pool of tears. She hears a long tale and takes advice from a caterpillar. Then she reaches the Queen's croquet-ground, the Mock Turtle's story, and the trial over stolen tarts. Readers get the Wonderland story at its first stage, in Carroll's own hand and pictures, a treasure for lovers of the book and for students of how it grew.
19759-address-by-honorable-franklin-k-la:
Franklin K. Lane served as Secretary of the Interior under President Wilson. This address of his deals with wartime highways transport work. It describes state committees grouped into eleven regional areas. Regional chairmen supervised those committees under the Highways Transport Committee. The Council of National Defense ran the structure. Lane's name gave the effort national weight.

Speeches by cabinet officers rallied local officials to national plans. Transport was one of the home front's hardest problems. Lane was known as a forceful, plain speaker on public questions. The address shows federal coordination reaching down to counties. It also shows how maps and regions organized the work. Such speeches are primary records of wartime administration.
20303-the-best-short-stories-of-1915-and:
The Best Short Stories of 1915 reprints the year's finest tales, with a yearbook. Permissions came from The Masses, Collier's Weekly, and many other sources. Chautonville, La Dernière Mobilisation, and The Citizen are among the tales. Editors thanked each magazine and author for the right to reprint.

A yearbook of the American short story rides with the tales. It lists stories, authors, and magazines in a useful record. Annual best volumes shaped taste and careers in fiction then. Readers get a rich cross-section of American short fiction in wartime 1915.
2038-the-lock-and-key-library-classic-my:
Julian Hawthorne edits this 1909 anthology of classic mystery and detective stories by modern English writers, including Kipling, Conan Doyle, Weyman, Collins, and Stevenson. The volume opens with Kipling's ghost story of India. Hawthorne's series appeared in 1909, when detective fiction was moving from magazines to book shelves.

Tales of murder, detection, and the uncanny follow, chosen to show the range of the form at its best. For readers new to Victorian mystery, the collection serves as a strong first shelf, with famous names beside lesser-known gems. The English volume balances famous authors with lesser tales, so a reader meets both masters and surprises.
20872-the-best-short-stories-of-1917-and:
Thanks to The Century Magazine and Scribner's fill the credits of The Best Short Stories of 1917. Edward O'Brien picked the year's finest tales for this yearly set. Thomas Beer's Onnie and Maxwell Struthers Burt's A Cup of Tea stand among the choices.

A yearbook of the American short story closes the volume with lists and notes. O'Brien tracked the field's health with charts of tales by magazine and author. Such sets guided readers to the best new fiction of the year. This one freezes 1917's story craft just as America entered the Great War.
20917-the-cultivation-of-the-native-grap:
Leif, son of Eric the Red, bought a ship and crewed it with thirty-five men in the year 1000. George Husmann quotes that old voyage in The Cultivation of the Native Grape. A German, Tyrker, sailed with Leif from Iceland in that famed crew.

Husmann, a Missouri grape pioneer, teaches vine choice, pruning, and wine making in full. Native grapes that beat rot and frost stand at his work's core. His book helped build American wine craft in the Midwest and beyond. Growers still cite his plain, tested counsel, born of decades among his own vines at Hermann.
21402-our-sailors-gallant-deeds-of-the-b:
Bold deeds by British sailors fill W. H. G. Kingston's Our Sailors, a record of the navy in Queen Victoria's reign. Kingston wrote the book early in his career and died in 1880, well before the queen. Friends brought the tale up to date after his death, with help linked to G. A. Henty.

Many of the tales are, in truth, land fights backed by naval force. Sailors hauled guns ashore and stood in the line at sieges and reliefs. The relief of Mafeking is one such famed case. The book shows how far the Victorian navy reached, on sea and land alike.
21483-the-wanderers-or-adventures-in-the:
The Macnamara family leaves Pennsylvania for Trinidad in W. H. G. Kingston's The Wanderers. Dennis Macnamara, a thriving merchant, had raised them in comfort with Uncle Paul and cousin Arthur at hand. Politics drives them out, and they choose Trinidad, a choice Kingston calls a big mistake.

Spanish priests rule the island's faith with a hard hand, and the mother's burial sparks a clash. The family flees to South America and pushes up the Orinoco River. Perils crowd the wilds there, and Spanish rule bars their way again. News of a kinder regime in Trinidad at last calls them home.
21655-the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-vol:
Volume five of Maupassant's works holds Une Vie, A Woman's Life, in a 1909 English edition. Edmund Gosse introduces the author, a Norman of old family, born at the Château de Miromesnil in 1850. Flaubert, the great Norman master, shaped the young writer's art.

Une Vie follows a woman's hopes from youth into a hard, narrowing life. Shorter tales fill the rest: Hautot Senior and Hautot Junior, Little Louise Roqué, and A Passion. Gosse notes the tales' brilliant craft and audacious tone. One tale in the French set drew threats of prosecution, which only secured the book's fortune and fame.
22091-the-best-short-stories-of-1920-and:
Edward J. O'Brien edited the yearly Best Short Stories volumes, and the 1920 book surveys stories printed in 1919. O'Brien read the magazines of America hunting for real literature among the fiction. His yearbook section lists stories, authors, and magazines in careful detail. The roll of honour names the year's finest work, judged by his strict standards.

Sherwood Anderson stands among the writers whose work the volume records. So do editors and publishers from Scribner's, Collier's, and the Cosmopolitan, thanked for their help. The series helped fix the short story's place in American letters. Libraries still use O'Brien's yearbooks to trace what the magazines printed and what one demanding editor valued.
23046-the-comedy-of-errors-the-works-of-:
A death sentence opens The Comedy of Errors in this Cambridge Shakespeare text. Merchant of Syracusa, plead no more, the Duke tells old Egeon. No partiality, the Duke rules, will bend Ephesus's laws for a Syracusan merchant. The enmity between the cities, sealed with merchants' blood, excludes all pity from our threatening looks.

Inside that grim frame spins Shakespeare's fastest farce, two sets of twins, one town, and a day of mistaken doors and dinners. Egeon's sad story gives the romp real stakes. The Cambridge edition presents the play with its scholarly notes, the fruit of collating the Folio text. Readers can watch a perfect comic machine and study how editors keep it wound. Few first plays by anyone run this cleanly.
23391-sally-of-missouri:
R. E. Young wrote this nineteen hundred three novel of Sally Madeira, a Missouri girl whose life runs from New York steering rooms to pine woods, boom towns, and the garden of dreams. Chapters trace her growth, her father's hopes, and the town Jack built, where boom time brings both fortune and folly.

Sally finds herself through work, love, and loss, as meals run out, mistakes pile up, and a sweetheart's fate hangs in the balance. Young writes with warmth and a keen eye for small town talk, mining camps, and the push of new wealth. Readers who like a heroine with grit will enjoy Sally's rise, as she learns to steer her own course through a changing West.
23445-the-best-short-stories-of-1919-and:
Edward J. O'Brien edited this yearbook of the American short story, gathering the best tales of nineteen nineteen with notes on the year's work. Earlier volumes for nineteen fifteen through nineteen eighteen had set the pattern, and this book keeps it, with copyrights from magazines and book houses across the land.

Sherwood Anderson, Djuna Barnes, James Branch Cabell, Susan Glaspell, Joseph Hergesheimer, and many more appear, their stories picked for craft and force. O'Brien's yearbook notes trace trends, praise new voices, and record where each tale first ran. Readers who love the short story will find a rich survey of a single year's best American fiction, plus a guide to the writers and journals that shaped it.
23668-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Gleeson White wrote this volume of Bell's Cathedrals series on Salisbury Cathedral, first published in December 1896 and revised with eighteen added illustrations in 1898. With fifty illustrations in all, it describes the cathedral's fabric — its stonework, plan, and fittings — and pairs that architectural account with a brief history of the See of Sarum.

Readers walk the building as White explains what they see, from the bishop's palace view to the details of nave and choir. The history places Salisbury among England's great medieval churches. It serves both visitors planning a trip and readers at home who want to understand how a Gothic cathedral was built and how its diocese grew.
24829-the-uses-of-italic-a-primer-of-inf:
Frederick W. Hamilton wrote this primer in 1918 for the Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices, issued by the United Typothetae of America. It tells young printers where italic letters came from and how to use them right, from book titles and ship names to foreign phrases and scientific terms.

The history opens with Gothic black letter, then follows smaller books and faster presses, from Gutenberg's twenty sheets an hour to the presses of 1786. Review questions close the book, testing rules for citations, footnotes, and plays. The primer remains a clear, short guide to a craft rule that still shapes printed pages.
24947-medi-val-wales-chiefly-in-the-twel:
A. G. Little's six popular lectures, published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1902, survey medieval Wales chiefly in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The opening lecture frames the theme as a failure: Wales never effected a stable and lasting political combination, and Little traces that shortfall through chronicle, castle, and cloister. Geoffrey of Monmouth and Giraldus Cambrensis receive their own lectures as the storytellers who shaped how Wales saw itself.

Castles and religious houses get full treatment, with maps and plans of Cardiff and Caerphilly among them, before the final lecture turns to Llywelyn ap Gruffydd and the Barons' War. Gerald's audience with Innocent III supplies a human touch, with the pope laughing at tales of an archbishop's bad Latin. The lectures stay clear and popular in aim, a sound entry to Welsh history.
25084-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
G. H. Palmer's Cathedral Church of Rochester, published by George Bell and Sons in 1897, is a visitor's guide to one of England's oldest cathedrals. It belongs to Bell's Cathedral series, planned to give tourists accurate, well-illustrated handbooks at a popular price without drowning them in technical terms.

Palmer describes the building stone by stone, from Gundulf's tower and the transepts to Sir George Gilbert Scott's Victorian restorations, and adds a brief history of the bishopric. The volume suits both the casual visitor walking the nave and the student of medieval architecture tracing how the fabric changed across eight centuries.
25305-memoirs-of-fanny-hill-a-new-and-ge:
John Cleland's Memoirs of Fanny Hill, first published in London in 1749, is one of the most famous and most prosecuted novels in English. This Paris edition, privately printed by Isidore Liseux in 350 numbered copies, claims a genuine text from the original.

Fanny writes letters to a friend, recalling her life from country innocence through London's underworld to love, health, and fortune. Cleland tells the story with wit and a sharp eye for manners, which is why the book survived bans and trials to become a literary classic as well as a scandal.
26367-the-young-alaskans-on-the-missouri:
Emerson Hough's 1922 boys' novel sends the Young Alaskans up the Missouri in the wake of Lewis and Clark. The boys sail in a boat named Adventurer, and Hough quotes the explorers' own orders, mess lists, and journal entries as they plan each stage. Chapters follow the river from its lower reaches toward the Platte and beyond.

Wreck, a lost hunter, and meetings with Sioux and Mandan people mark the journey, along with stops at the Yellowstone, the Great Falls, and the Three Forks. The party pushes on to the utmost source of the river, fishes for grayling, and ends at a ranch before turning home. History and outdoor adventure share the pages in equal measure.
27307-the-last-american-a-fragment-from-:
J. A. Mitchell's The Last American, a fragment from the journal of Khan-Li, Prince of Dimph-Yoo-Chur and Admiral in the Persian Navy, appeared in an edition de luxe from Stokes in 1889. It was illustrated by F. W. Read. It is dedicated to thoughtful Persians who can learn from a foolish people's swift fall after a sudden rise.

Hedful, curator of the Imperial Museum at Shiraz, presents Khan-Li's discoveries among the Mehrikan people. European comers grew flat-chested and thin, their hair scanty, their teeth fragile, and their digestions weak. Between 1945 and 1960 the last census found a sleeping continent and, in soft earth, the imprint of human feet.
28687-the-only-true-mother-goose-melodie:
Munroe and Francis of Boston published this 1833 collection of Mother Goose rhymes, claiming it as the only true text without addition or abridgement. It also promises a reliable life of the Goose family, never before published, and many illustrations. Mother Goose herself speaks in the preface, scolding rival grannies who want her soothing rhymes laid aside for more learned books.

The rhymes inside are the familiar nursery songs, presented as an anodyne for cross, peevish children who will not be comforted. This edition matters because it fixed an early American form of Mother Goose, defending nursery verse against critics who thought it too silly for children. Readers get both the rhymes and a lively piece of publishing history, in the voice of Ma'am Goose herself.
30206-humanity-s-gain-from-unbelief-repr:
Charles Bradlaugh argues that humanity has gained from unbelief, in an essay reprinted from the North American Review of March 1889. He pleads, as an unbeliever, that the slow rejection of Christianity, like the rejection of earlier faiths, has added to human happiness and well-being. Science, he says, grows from scepticism, and general progress stalls where religion forbids doubt about the supernatural.

Freethought Publishing issued the London pamphlet in 1889, and Bradlaugh writes as a Monist, using nature to mean all phenomena and all that makes any event happen. Religions, he holds, change with the peoples who hold them, and each discovery breaks some cherished belief in whole or part. Short and direct, the essay states the Victorian freethought case in its clearest form.
31384-in-the-early-days-along-the-overla:
Gilbert L. Cole's 1905 memoir, compiled by Mrs. A. Hardy and published in Kansas City, tells an overland trip through Nebraska Territory in 1852, fifty-three years before publication. Testimonials from Beatrice citizens praise it as a true story plainly told and a vivid portrayal of conditions. They call it a valuable contribution to the meager literature of a time near in years but distant in conditions.

Twelve chapters move from setting up altars of remembrance through prairies as a book, a worthy object reached for, and a snowbank's tears. They go on to stepping over the ridge, having no flag to unfurl, listening to each other, boots and saddles, and all coming right in the end. Plain and firsthand, the book preserves a pioneer's memory of the trail before Nebraska was a state.
31770-the-struggle-for-missouri:
John McElroy's 1909 history, published by the National Tribune in Washington and dedicated to the Union men of Missouri, tells how Missouri became a battleground over slavery. He argues that Southern statesmen of the elder school planned a separate government with slavery as its cornerstone, aiming to dominate the continent and absorb Cuba, Mexico, and Central America.

The book opens with Missouri's 1818 boundaries and the Ordinance of 1787, which had dedicated the Northwest to freedom. It follows the political struggle that made the state a salient bastion of the slavery empire. Readers get a partisan but detailed Civil War-era history from a Union point of view.
31974-last-days-of-the-rebellion-the-sec:
Alanson M. Randol's 1886 account Last Days of the Rebellion follows the Second New York Cavalry, Harris' Light, at Appomattox Station and Appomattox Court House on April 8 and 9, 1865. Randol, major of the First U. S. Artillery and late colonel of the Second New York, wrote from Alcatraz Island, California.

During the winter of 1864 to 1865 the regiment lay in winter quarters near Winchester, Virginia, on the Romney pike, in the first brigade, third division, cavalry corps, under General George A. Custer's division and A. C. M. Pennington's brigade. On February 27, 1865, Merritt's and Custer's divisions, with Miller's and Woodruff's batteries, all under General Sheridan, left winter quarters. Readers get a cavalry officer's account of the war's final days.
32228-the-indian-captive-a-narrative-of-:
Matthew Brayton's Indian Captive, published at Fostoria, Ohio, by the Gray Printing Company in 1896, tells of thirty-four years of captivity among the Indians of north-western America. Its first chapter, The Lost Child, sets the scene in north-western Ohio, south-east of the Black Swamp, near the end of the first quarter of the century. Hardy pioneers from New England built modest dwellings there and tilled acres won from dense forest and luxuriant prairie.

The Indians, driven from all other parts of Ohio, clung to that comparatively neglected spot, and the settler's smoke rose where the Indian wigwam stood in view. The two races were at peace, Brayton writes, for neither cared to turn a passive neighbour into an active enemy. Readers get a frontier captivity narrative, beginning with a lost child and stretching across more than three decades among the Indians.
3240-cap-n-eri:
Joseph Crosby Lincoln sets this Cape Cod novel around Captain Eri and his household. A lamb for the sacrifice opens the chapters, then the train comes in and the come-outers hold their meeting. A picture sent and a cable tested, a woman from Nantucket, and the schoolhouse bell ringing follow. Captain Eri finds a nurse, and housekeeper and book agent take their turns.

Elsie Preston, matchmaking and life-saving, heroes and a mystery, and a little politics fill the later chapters. Captain Jerry makes a mess of things before the voyage of an able seaman closes the local drama. Lincoln writes his village with affection and a keen ear. Boarding houses, town meetings, and neighbors' plans that rarely survive contact with one another carry the comedy.
32405-augusta-triumphans-or-the-way-to-m:
Andrew Moreton's pamphlet sets out a plan to make London the most flourishing city in the universe, in a second edition dated 1729 and reprinted at Oxford in 1841. Its six proposals begin with a university where gentlemen may study under the eye of their friends, a hospital for foundlings, and an academy of sciences at Christ's Hospital. Moreton also calls for closing pretended madhouses where women are unjustly confined.

Further proposals aim to save youth from ruin by clearing streets of vice, gaming tables, and Sunday debauchery. Others aim to save the lower classes from ruin by curbing the immoderate use of Geneva, or gin. The pamphlet closes with a method to prevent street robberies and a letter on the orphans' tax. It reads as a bold, practical reform tract from early Georgian London.
32548-rambling-recollections-of-chelsea-:
An Old Inhabitant's Rambling Recollections of Chelsea, transcribed from a 1901 Press Printers edition, recalls Chelsea as a village in the early part of the past century. The author, writing from Highfield Lodge, Wandsworth Common, in June 1901, compiled recollections from a diary kept only now and then, while confined to a room to pass weary hours. Friends and neighbours, he hoped, would enjoy the souvenir of old friendship.

Early Chelsea, he recalls, had village industries now entirely passed away. Villagers rode the Village Clock, a two-horse stage coach running twice daily between the Cross Keys, Lawrence Street, and Charing Cross for one shilling. A picture of the Old Swan, Chelsea, heads the volume. Readers get a warm, detailed local history of streets, shops, coaches, and neighbours before London swallowed the village.
33793-the-seven-branched-candlestick-the:
Gilbert W. Gabriel recalls the schooldays of a young American Jew in this 1925 volume, copyrighted in 1917. The narrator counts seven school years, none altogether happy but none lean: two at high school, one at a military school on the Hudson, and four at his city's university. Each year, he writes, is a lighted candle in the dark of the past, and seven together form the seven-branched candlestick, a stately and reverent symbol of his faith.

Twenty chapters move from a prologue and beginning through Friday night, the boy and the school, the military academy, a Steerforth figure, freshman year, within the gates, an aunt. The memoir blends education, identity, and coming of age with warmth and candor.
33948-the-hollow-tree-snowed-in-book-bei:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote this continuation of his Hollow Tree tales, published by Harper in 1910 with pictures by J. M. Conde. The Hollow Tree and Deep Woods people return: Mr. Crow, Mr. Turtle, Mr. Coon, Mr. Possum, Mr. Robin, Mr. Squirrel, Mr. Dog, and Mr. Rabbit. Snow shuts them in, and their winter doings fill the book.

A map of the Hollow Tree country opens the volume, with the top marked south, as the tree folk always have it. Tales of a menagerie visit and other winter scrapes follow in Paine's gentle voice. The book is a cozy winter companion to the earlier Hollow Tree volume.
3657-wild-beasts-and-their-ways-reminisc:
Samuel White Baker writes hunting reminiscences from Europe, Asia, Africa, and America in this volume. Baker, famous for his Nile explorations, turns here to wild beasts and their ways. He describes how lions, elephants, tigers, bears, and other game live, feed, and defend themselves, and how a hunter meets them in the field. His stories span continents and decades of travel.

Baker writes as a Victorian sportsman, full of incident and practical detail about rifles, tracking, and camp life. Modern readers will note attitudes toward hunting that belong to his time. The book suits those interested in natural history, exploration, and the age when a traveler could still meet great beasts in wild country.
4631-the-hand-but-not-the-heart-or-the-l:
T. S. Arthur published The Hand but Not the Heart, or The Life-Trials of Jessie Loring, in 1858. It opens in a drawing room, where Paul Hendrickson starts at his name, a delicate flush on his handsome face, as Mrs. Denison remarks on his absent-minded air. She has watched him standing like a statue. He, assuming an indifference he plainly does not feel, denies that half an hour has passed since he came to that part of the room.

The title points to the book's trial: a hand given in marriage without the heart behind it, and the life that follows such a bargain. Arthur follows Jessie Loring through courtship, marriage, and the daily tests of affection, duty, and pride. Readers get a domestic novel of its day, earnest and readable, about what happens when the forms of love are kept while its feeling is withheld.
7485-the-last-american-a-fragment-from-t:
J. A. Mitchell's satire of 1889 imagines America extinct and explored by Persians. The fragment is presented as the journal of Khan-Li, prince of Dimph-Yoo-Chur and admiral in the Persian navy, introduced by Hedful, curator of the Imperial Museum at Shiraz. The explorers find the ruins of a people who rose suddenly and vanished swiftly, and the book is dedicated to thoughtful Persians who can read a warning in that fate.

Mitchell uses the future explorer's eye to satirize his own age: its nervous energy, its imitation of other nations, its extravagance, and its thin patriotism, as the Persian narrator judges them. The satire bites because the ruins are familiar: American cities, customs, and boasts seen through foreign eyes. The Last American is an early work of future-history fiction, funny and sharp.
a-conspiracy-of-the-carbonari: Luise Muhlbach tells of a conspiracy of the Carbonari after the battle of Essling. The novel opens on the evening of May 22, 1809, the day that first dimmed Napoleon's star. A father shows his daughter Leonore ten banknotes of fifty thousand francs each, calling them magic spells. Muhlbach weaves secret societies, money, and Napoleonic politics into a historical romance.
alice-s-adventures-under-ground-being-a-: Lewis Carroll presents a facsimile of his original manuscript book, Alice's Adventures Under Ground, later developed into Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. The hand-written text, with thirty-seven of the author's own illustrations, shows the tale in its first, shorter form. It is a treasure for Carroll lovers, revealing how a story told to a child grew into a classic.
amos-kilbright-his-adscititious-experien: Frank R. Stockton tells of Amos Kilbright and his adscititious experiences, with other stories including a reversible landscape and dusky philosophy in two expositions. Stockton's humour turns on odd notions taken to their logical end, with a light, inventive touch. The collection shows why he was a favourite maker of American comic tales.
an-enquiry-concerning-the-principles-of-: Frances Reynolds enquires into the principles of taste and the origin of our ideas of beauty. Her essay argues about how we judge what is fine, and where our sense of beauty comes from. As a woman theorist of art in the eighteenth century, Reynolds offers a rare, thoughtful voice on aesthetics.
an-unwilling-maid-being-the-history-of-c: Jeanie Gould Lincoln tells the history of certain episodes during the American Revolution in the early life of Mistress Betty Yorke, born Wolcott, an unwilling maid. The chapters follow Miss Moppet, bullets for defence, and Oliver's prisoner, as a girl meets war with spirit. Addressed to a nineteenth-century girl, the book makes history personal and lively.
b09-melanchthon-de-obitu-lutheri:
De obitu Martini Lutheri is the funeral oration Philipp Melanchthon gave for Martin Luther at Wittenberg. Luther died in February 1546, and Melanchthon spoke over him on February 19, before the gathered university and town. The Latin oration served as the Reformation's public farewell to its founder.

Melanchthon traces Luther's life, teaching, and trials, and praises the gifts God gave the church through him. Grief runs through the speech, held in check by a scholar's order. The text also fixes an early, near account of how Luther's own circle wished him remembered. It remains a moving close to the first age of the Reformation.
britannica-1911-a-fortiori: A fortiori, a Latin phrase meaning from a stronger reason, names a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry defines an argument that proves a point through a stronger case that already covers it. If A is shown less than B, and A is known greater than C, then C falls below B with no fresh proof. Where the ground is only likelihood, as in the Gospel saying the entry cites, the move rests on common sense rather than strict proof.
britannica-1911-a-priori:
A priori, from what comes before, receives a compact entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the phrase two lives: common speech for a judgment made without fresh facts, and logic, where Albert of Saxony first used it. Aristotle's order of cause and effect stands behind both.

Nature puts causes first, while human learning starts from facts, the entry explains. Kant recast the pair as kinds of judgment: a priori, free of sense reports, and a posteriori, drawn from them. Camps of Intuitionalist and Empiricist fought over the line. The entry ends in truce: pure a priori thought is form without content, and all real knowing mixes mind with fact.
britannica-1911-abba-mari:
Abba Mari receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abba Mari ben Moses, called Astruc of Lunel, was a French rabbi born near Montpellier late in the thirteenth century. Talmud, Maimonides, and Nachmanides formed his learning, in a house of learned men.

At Montpellier he fought the spread of Aristotelian reason drawn from Maimonides, fearing for law, miracle, and revelation. His letters, gathered as Minhat Kenaot, called Solomon ben Adret of Barcelona to orthodoxy's aid. A ban on philosophy study under age thirty followed in 1305, and schism followed the ban. Driven from France in 1306, he settled at Perpignan and printed the letters. Verse and civil law works stand to his name as well.
britannica-1911-abu-l-ala-ul-ma-arri:
Abu-l-'Ala ul-Ma'arri (973-1057) was an Arabian poet and letter-writer from Ma'arrat un-Nu'man in Syria, south of Aleppo. Blinded by smallpox at the age of four, he still studied under leading teachers at Aleppo, Antioch, and Tripoli. A stay in Baghdad brought him into its literary circles before he returned home to teach and write.

Two collections of poems and two of letters carry his name. The later poems, the Luzumiyyat, use a hard double-consonant rhyme and turn pessimistic, reflecting on change, virtue, and death. His letters treat literary and social subjects, and one set deals with his vegetarian views. Readers meet a blind scholar whose memory and independence set him apart.
britannica-1911-bakhtiari:
Bakhtiari are one of Persia's great nomad tribes. Their camping grounds fill a hilly province. It runs from Chaharmahal toward Shushter. The Dizful river bounds it northward. Behbahan and Ram Hormuz touch it southward. Two great divisions split the tribe.

Haft-lang and Chahar-lang are those divisions. Many branches and clans follow them. Until the 1400s they were the Great Lurs. Their speech is the Lur language. It is a Persian dialect. They number some 38,000 to 40,000 families. That means under 200,000 souls in all. Their district covers about 25,000 square miles. Mid-century they could field 20,000 horsemen. Feuds and misrule have shrunk that strength. Perhaps 4,000 horsemen remain available now. Their chiefs lately improved the Isfahan road. Iron bridges now cross the Karun there.
britannica-1911-bakri:
Bakri (1040-1094) was an Arabian geographer of Spain. His full name runs Abdallah ibn Abd ul-Aziz ul-Bakri. Cordova was his birthplace and home. His best-known work is a dictionary of names. It covers geographical names found in the poets. Such names often puzzle readers of old verse.

An introduction treats the Arabian tribes' seats. It sets out where each tribe lived. Wüstenfeld edited the dictionary at Göttingen. The edition ran through 1876 and 1877. Another work was a general world geography. That book survives only in manuscript form. Its North Africa part was edited separately. De Slane published it at Algiers in 1857. Brockelmann's history of Arabic literature gives more detail. It treats Bakri among the geographers of his age.
britannica-1911-balikisri:
Balikisri, also spelled Balukiser, was a town of Asia Minor, chief town of the Karasi sanjak in the vilayet of Brusa. It stands 575 feet up, on rising ground above a fertile plain that drains toward the Sea of Marmora. Its people numbered about 20,000, most of them Moslems, with some 5,000 Christians.

Trade in opium, silk, and grain centred on the town, linked by carriage roads to Panderma. The 1911 Britannica entry notes silver mines worked at Balia and boracite mines at Susurlu, signs of the district's mineral wealth. On or near the site stood the Roman town of Hadrianutherae, founded by the emperor Hadrian.
britannica-1911-beri-beri:
Beri-beri is a tropical disease of the greatest age, known to the Chinese from very early times. It faded from European sight until an outbreak in Brazil in 1863 and study in Japan and Borneo brought it back. Work by Scheube and Bälz in Japan and by Pekelharing and Winkler in the Dutch Indies described it as a form of peripheral neuritis, a wasting of the nerves.

The disease ranges between 45 degrees north and 35 south: Japan, Korea, the China coast, Burma, Java, Ceylon and East Africa, and across to Cuba, Panama and South America. Ships have carried it as far as Australia and London. Many authorities of the day blamed an infective parasite, though none had been surely found; the young, from fifteen to forty, suffer most.
britannica-1911-bihari:
Bihari is the most western of the four languages in the Eastern Group of modern Indo-Aryan tongues. The others are Bengali, Oriya, and Assamese. The 1911 Britannica article, signed by Grierson, counts 34,579,844 Bihari speakers in British India in 1901. The whole group then numbered over ninety million. Bihari is also spoken in the Tarai districts of Nepal. Its name means the language of the province of Bihar.

The article traces Bihari to the old Magadhi Prakrit of South Bihar. It maps the speech far beyond the province, west past Benares and south over Chota Nagpur. Dialects such as Bhojpuri and Magahi get detailed treatment. Grammar, sounds, and literature are worked through at great length. Long lists of authorities close the piece. It is a technical survey for language students, not a general sketch.
britannica-1911-bolgari:
Bolgari, or Bolgary, is a ruined town in the Russian government of Kazan, 4 miles from the left bank of the Volga. It is generally taken to have been the capital of the Bulgarians in that region from the 400s to the 1400s. Old walls and towers still stand on the site.

Burial mounds around it hold inscriptions in Arabic, Armenian, and Turkic, and dug tombs gave up weapons, tools, dishes, and silver and copper coins. Finds gathered from 1722 sit in museums at Kazan, Moscow, and St Petersburg. Mongols wrecked the city in 1238 and Tamerlane wrecked it again a century later. It then served the khans of the Golden Horde before passing to the principality of Kazan in the late 1400s.
britannica-1911-boulainvilliers-henri:
Henri, comte de Boulainvilliers (1658–1722), was a French political writer who praised the feudal order without reserve. Born at St Saire in Normandy and schooled at Juilly, he served in the army until 1697. All his books came out after his death, among them histories of France's old government and of the peerage, and a history of the Arabs.

He was an aristocrat of the strongest type, the entry says, attacking absolute monarchy on one side and popular government on the other. He worked hard to prove his own family's ancient nobility and held that rule should rest solely with men of his class. His Histoire de l'ancien gouvernement de la France and his État de la France, both printed in 1727, carried his feudal argument across Europe. He died in Paris in 1722.
britannica-1911-brisson-eugene-henri:
Eugene Henri Brisson (born 1835) was a French statesman born at Bourges on 31 July 1835. Trained as an advocate like his father, he stood out in opposition during the last days of the empire and became deputy-mayor of Paris after its fall. Voters sent him to the Assembly on 8 February 1871 as a member of the extreme Left.

He backed obligatory primary schooling and fought clerical power, and he was first to propose an amnesty for the condemned of the Commune in September 1871, though the vote went against him. President of the chamber from 1881 to March 1885, he succeeded Jules Ferry as prime minister, then resigned after barely winning a credit vote for the Tongking expedition. Later he helped expose the Panama scandals, nearly won the presidency after Carnot's murder in 1894, and headed a cabinet in June 1898 amid the Dreyfus affair.
britannica-1911-buccari:
Buccari is a royal free town of Croatia-Slavonia, in Hungary. Its Serbo-Croatian name is Bakar. It stands seven miles south-east of Fiume. The town sits on a small bay of the Adriatic Sea. Its population in 1900 was 1870. This 1911 Britannica entry describes its trade and harbour.

The harbour gives good anchorage to small vessels. Its approach can be dangerous, though. Rivalry from Fiume cost Buccari most of its trade in the 19th century. Boatbuilding is now the staple industry. A coasting trade runs in fish, wine, wood and coal. The tunny fishery also brings in money. The state railway ends about two and a half miles away. Near the town stands the old castle of Buccarica. Farther south lies the small port of Porto Ré, or Kraljevica.
britannica-1911-capri:
Capri is an island on the south side of the Bay of Naples. Its ancient name was Capreae. This 1911 Britannica entry describes it in detail. It lies about 20 miles south of the town of Naples. It forms part of the province of Naples. The commune of Capri held 3890 people in 1901. Anacapri, the second town, held 2316. The island is 4 miles long and covers 5.5 square miles.

Monte Solaro, the highest point, rises 1920 feet. The east cliffs drop 900 feet sheer to the sea. The only safe landing is on the north side. Two towns, Capri and Anacapri, stand at different heights. A flight of 784 steps joined them until 1874. A carriage road then replaced the climb. The island lacks water and is dusty in drought. Still, it yields fruit, wine and olive oil. Some 30,000 visitors came each year, drawn by the scenery.
britannica-1911-carbonari:
The Carbonari were secret revolutionary societies in Italy and France. Their name is Italian for “charcoal-burners.” This long 1911 Britannica article traces their history. They played an active part early in the 19th century. Stories linking them to medieval brotherhoods are pure fancy. The entry calls those tales fantastic and dismisses them. The Carbonari were probably an offshoot of the Freemasons.

They first gained weight in southern Italy. That was during the Napoleonic wars in Europe. Under Murat's reign, from 1808 to 1815, secret societies multiplied. Their aim was to free Italy from foreign rule. They also sought constitutional liberties for the people. They would back the Bourbons or Murat, if either delivered. Their watchwords were freedom and independence for Italy. But they agreed on no single form of government. The article follows their plots, risings and suppression in turn.
britannica-1911-carthage-missouri:
Carthage is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city and the county-seat of Jasper county, Missouri, on the Spring river about 150 miles south by east of Kansas City. Its population was 9483 in the census of 1910. Three railways serve the city, and an electric line links it with Webb City, Joplin, and Galena in Kansas. The town stands on high ground over solid limestone, near 950 feet above sea level.

Lead, zinc, and coal mines and quarries of Carthage “marble” lie in the neighbourhood, and the county court house is built of that stone. The city jobs goods for a fruit and grain region and makes lime, flour, furniture, bed springs, mining machinery, ploughs, and woollen goods. Factory products in 1905 were worth $1,179,661. Founded in 1833, Carthage became the county-seat in 1842. A Presbyterian collegiate institute, a yearly Chautauqua assembly, and a county fair complete the picture.
britannica-1911-casamari:
Casamari is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Cistercian abbey in the province of Rome, six miles east south east of Veroli. The abbey marks the site of Cereatae, the birthplace of Marius. Inscriptions show the place was later known as Cereatae Marianae. It stood as an independent community under the early empire, perhaps cut from the territory of Arpinum by the triumvirs.

The building itself is the entry's chief point. Casamari is a fine example of Burgundian early Gothic work, dated 1203 to 1217. In Italy only Fossanuova, built at almost the same time, stands beside it. The abbey survives very well preserved. A cited study by C. Enlart on the French origins of Gothic architecture in Italy points readers to the wider argument about how this style crossed the Alps.
britannica-1911-chieri:
Chieri is a town and episcopal see of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Turin, 13 miles south-east of Turin by rail. Its people numbered 11,929 in the town and 13,803 in the commune in 1901. The Gothic cathedral, founded in 1037 and rebuilt in 1405, is the largest in Piedmont. A 13th century octagonal baptistery stands with it, and the town's past runs through bishops, counts and the house of Savoy.

Chieri was subject to the bishop of Turin in the 9th and 10th centuries, then became independent in the 11th century. In 1347 it submitted by choice to Count Amedeus VI of Savoy to escape the marquis of Monferrato. Savoy rule became final in the 16th century, and in 1785 the town was made a principality of the duke of Aosta. Trade and making came early, and by the mid 15th century it produced about 100,000 pieces of cotton goods a year.
britannica-1911-chillicothe-missouri:
Chillicothe is a city and the county-seat of Livingston county, Missouri, in the north of the state on the Grand river, about 80 miles north-east of Kansas City. Its people numbered 6,905 in 1900 and 6,265 in 1910, after 5,717 in 1890. Three railways serve the city, the Chicago, Milwaukee and St Paul, the Wabash and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy. Manufactures of various kinds are carried on there, the entry notes.

Coal and limestone are found in the vicinity, and much live stock is raised around the city. Wool and hides are shipped from Chillicothe as farm products of the district. Settlers came about 1830, and the town was laid out in 1837 on land granted directly by the Federal government. Incorporation followed in 1855. Rail links, minerals and stock raising together explain the town's place in its county.
britannica-1911-fatehpur-sikri:
Fatehpur Sikri is a town in the Agra district of the United Provinces of India, on the road from Agra to Jaipur, with 7,147 people in 1901. It is a ruined city of interest chiefly for its buildings. Akbar founded it in 1569 as a thank-offering for the birth of his son Selim, later the emperor Jahangir. The saint Selim Chisti had foretold that birth.

Its great mosque, said to be hardly surpassed in India, holds the white marble tomb of Selim Chisti, with pierced stone tracery. Other buildings include the palace of Jodh Bai, the five-storeyed Panch Mahal and Akbar's private apartments. The soft red sandstone could be carved almost like wood. Deserted within fifty years for lack of good water, the walled city keeps its carved fabric in ruin.
britannica-1911-gregoire-henri:
Henri Gregoire (1750-1831) was a French revolutionist and constitutional bishop of Blois, born at Veho near Luneville on 4 December 1750. The 1911 Britannica entry treats him as one of the Revolution's most principled churchmen. Note: his hosted file opens with the bibliography of the preceding article, on the Gregarines, before his own entry begins.

Gregoire's fame rests on his stand for the civil rights of Jews and of men of colour. It rests, too, on his work for the abolition of slavery in the French colonies. As bishop of Blois under the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, he held his see through the Revolution's storms. The entry follows his long public life, his scholarship, and his refusal to bend under later regimes. He stands in the volume as the priest who tried to wed the Church to the Revolution's best promises.
britannica-1911-guarnieri:
The Guarnieri were a celebrated family of violin-makers. They worked at Cremona. Andreas, the first, lived about 1626 to 1698. He worked beside Stradivari in Nicolo Amati's workshop. His son Joseph made instruments first like his father's. Later Joseph developed a style with a narrow waist. Another son, Peter of Cremona, settled at Mantua. A third, Peter of Venice, was also a fine maker.

The greatest of the family was Joseph del Gesù. He was Andreas' nephew and lived 1687 to 1745. His label bore the I.H.S. inscription, hence his title. Bold outline and massive build mark his work. He chased tone rather than visual perfection. His models vary greatly, showing constant experiment. Paganini's playing on a Joseph turned taste his way. Amateurs then favoured his robust tone over Amati sweetness. Many spurious instruments also flooded Europe after the middle of the 18th century.
britannica-1911-kansas-city-missouri:
Kansas City, Missouri, is a city of Jackson county, the second in size in the state. It stands where the Missouri and Kansas rivers meet, next to Kansas City, Kansas, and 235 miles west of St Louis. Its people numbered 132,716 in 1890, 163,752 in 1900, and 248,381 in 1910, among them many German, Irish, Swedish, and English born settlers.

Called the gateway to the Southwest, it is one of the great railway centres of the United States. A dozen lines serve it, among them the Union Pacific, the Missouri Pacific, the Santa Fé, and the Rock Island. Its rise in twenty years, from a river town to a quarter of a million people, is the spine of the piece.
britannica-1911-kashmiri:
Kashmiri, properly Kāśmīrī, is the name of the home language of the valley of Kashmir and the hills about it. Its segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Kashmir article. In the census of 1901 its speakers were returned at 1,007,957. By origin it is the most southern member of the Dard group of the Piśāca languages.

Its kin are Shīnā, spoken round Gilgit, and Kōhistānī, spoken in the Indus hills. The wider family also counts Khōwār, the speech of Chitral, and the Kāfir group, of which Bashgali is the chief. Of all these tongues Kashmiri alone has a literature, or even an alphabet of its own. It is also the only one counted in the census of India, so no sure figures exist for the rest.
britannica-1911-lacordaire-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste Henri Lacordaire (1802–1861), French ecclesiastic and orator, was born at Recey-sur-Ource on the 12th of March 1802. He studied at Dijon, where his gift for rhetoric brought him local fame in the advocates' debates, and went on to practise law in Paris. Reading Lamennais's Essai sur l'Indifférence convinced his ardent nature, and in 1823 he entered the seminary of Saint-Sulpice. Ordained four years later, he became almoner of the college Henri IV.

He was called to help Lamennais edit L'Avenir. The journal argued that Catholicism belonged with liberty, equality and fraternity rather than with dynasty. Rome condemned the new teaching in an encyclical. Lacordaire later went to Rome, took the habit of a preaching friar at the Minerva, and wrote his Mémoire for restoring the Dominicans in France . Back in France in 1841 he resumed preaching at Notre Dame.
britannica-1911-lafont-pierre-cheri:
Pierre Chéri Lafont (1797–1873), French actor, was born at Bordeaux on the 15th of May 1797. He gave up work as an assistant ship's doctor in the navy and went to Paris to study singing and acting. The director of the Vaudeville engaged him, and he made his début there in 1821 in La Somnambule; his good looks and excellent voice soon made him a public favourite. After years at the Nouveautés and the Vaudeville, the burning of the latter in 1838 sent him to England, where he married Jenny Colon at Gretna Green and was soon divorced.

Back in Paris he joined the Variétés and acted there for fifteen years. Further engagements at the Vaudeville and the Gaiété followed. He ended his brilliant career at the Gymnase, playing the noble father. He died in Paris on the 19th of April 1873.
cap-n-eri:
Joseph Crosby Lincoln set this novel in a Cape Cod village, where Captain Eri Hazeltine keeps house with two other retired sea captains, all bachelors and all set in their ways. The contents promise the trouble early: a lamb for the sacrifice, the train coming in, and, fifth, the woman from Nantucket. The captains' household cannot run itself, and the village watches them try.

A housekeeper is engaged, and Mrs. Snow's arrival from Nantucket reorders the house and its three old salts. Lincoln builds comedy from shipboard habits carried ashore: watches kept, orders given, and a cable tested like a ship's line. Eri, the lamb of the first chapter, finds himself the one marked out by fate and by the schoolhouse bell. It is a courtship novel in oilskins, and it made Lincoln's name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostini-agaz:
Agostini Agazzari, musical composer of Siena's noble families, was born 2 December 1578. He died probably 10 April 1640; his first working years served Emperor Matthias. Rome took him about 1600 to succeed Anerio as the German College's maestro di cappella. Later he served at St. Apollinaris and the Roman Seminary. His final musical education came from Viadana of Mantua.

Both men share credit for developing thoroughbass and teaching the correct method of figuring a bass. In 1630 he returned to Siena, becoming maestro of the cathedral, and died holding that post. He belonged to the Academy of Armonici Intronati and ranked among the Roman school's most fruitful composers. His many works include masses from 1596 to 1608, motets, Magnificats, and litanies, often republished and praised in Proske's Musica divina. He also wrote the drama Eumelio for a wedding in 1614.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alatri:
Alatri is an Italian bishopric under the Holy See's immediate jurisdiction, comprising seven towns in Rome province. Its closeness to Rome argues Christianity was taught there very early. This does not compel belief in local legends placing the conversion of Ferentino, Alatri, and neighbouring towns in the apostolic age. The route of Italy's earliest Gospel preachers remains unknown. The first bishop of Alatri met in history is Paschasius in 551, who accompanied Pope Vigilius to Constantinople during the Three Chapters controversy.

In Alatri's church of St. Mary Major is preserved a wooden Madonna statue, a splendid example of twelfth-century Roman art. Alatri counts 16 parishes and 77 churches, chapels, and oratories. It has 64 secular priests and 52 seminarians, with 42 regular clergy, 31 lay brothers, and 81 women religious. There are 30 confraternities, one boys' school with 87 pupils, and three girls' schools with 30 pupils. Its population is 24,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-se:
Alessandro Serpieri was an Italian priest, astronomer, and seismologist, born near Rimini in October 1823 and dead at Fiesole in February 1885. Educated by the Piarist fathers at Urbino, he entered their novitiate at Florence in 1838 and studied philosophy and the sciences at the Ximenian College and observatory. In 1846 he became professor of philosophy and physics at Urbino, and in 1848 he was ordained a priest, later rector of the college.

Serpieri's merit as an astronomer lay in watching shooting stars. His first treatise dates from 1847, and in August 1850 he found that the August meteors stream from a point near Gamma Persei, giving the Perseids their name. His greatest work was in seismology. His study of the earthquake of 12 March 1873 was called a model of scientific analysis by de Rossi, and it first used the idea of a seismic radiant. His masterwork treated the earthquake of March 1875 with 240 documents from a hundred places.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allori:
The Allori were Florentine painters spanning three generations. Angiolo di Cosimo, called Il Bronzino, was an able painter and poet, born at Monticello near Florence in 1502 and dead at Florence in 1572. A pupil of Raffaelino del Garbo and later of Jacopo da Pontormo, he assisted Pontormo and completed his unfinished works. He became court painter to Cosimo I, Grand Duke of Tuscany. Among his portraits are those of Dante and Petrarch.

His nephew Alessandro Allori, born at Florence in 1535 and dead there in 1607, was an able artist patronized by Grand Duke Francesco. Alessandro's son Cristofano Allori, known as Bronzino the Younger, was born at Florence in 1577 and dead there in 1621. A pupil of his father, of Santo di Tito, and of Cigoli, and of somewhat irregular life, he was a painter of talent in both figure and landscape. He ranked among the Florentine school's best colourists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselmo-bandu:
Anselmo Banduri, archaeologist and coin scholar, born 1671, died 1743. He joined the Benedictines young and studied at Naples, then Florence. Here he met Montfaucon, seeking Chrysostom manuscripts in Italy. Banduri served him well and was recommended to Cosimo III for a Pavia chair. It was suggested he be sent to Paris for preparation. After a short stay at Rome, Banduri went to Paris.

In 1711 he published at Paris his Imperium Orientale, an illustrated Byzantine work from medieval Greek manuscripts, some then first made known. He defended himself against Casimir Oudin, attacking from second-hand knowledge. In 1718 he published at Paris two volumes on coinage from Trajan to the last Palaeologi. Of this work Father Eckhel says it contains few important contributions. The bibliography he prefixed to it was reprinted by Fabricius at Hamburg in 1719. In 1715 he became an honorary member of the Academy of Inscriptions, and in 1724 Orléans librarian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antivari:
Antivari, an old Adriatic port facing Bari across the sea, served as the Catholic archbishop's seat in Montenegro. Its bishops claimed roots in the fifth century, with a firm see by the ninth and a refounding in the twelfth. Over the centuries the town passed from Greek emperors to a small Dalmatian republic, then to Serb kings, Hungary, and Venice.

Venetian rule brought nearly a century of peace and busy trade, until Ottoman forces besieged the town in 1538. Later treaties handed it to Montenegro, and in 1886 its archdiocese came directly under the Holy See. A decree of 1902 restored its old rank as primatial see of Dalmatia, closing the story of a small port caught between empires, faiths, and shifting borders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-alleg:
Antonio Allegri, called Correggio after his Lombard birthplace, was born in 1494 and died in 1534. A merchant's son, he left no writings, had no known teachers or pupils, and never courted great patrons. From 1518 to 1530 he worked chiefly at Parma, then returned to his native town for his final years.

His genius unfolded away from art centres, in tender Madonnas, myth scenes such as Danae, and the Madonna del Latte. Vasari, writing in 1542, found no portrait or sketch of him in Lombardy, so little trace had he left. The entry presents a quiet master whose soft light and grace made him, in its words, the Master of Parma.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-neri:
Florentine priest and chemist Antonio Neri, who died in 1614 after a life of which few details survive, wrote the book that long ruled the craft of glassmaking. He travelled in Italy and Holland gathering knowledge of how glass was made, coloured, and used to imitate precious stones. He published it as L'Arte Vetraria, the Art of Glassmaking, at Florence in 1612. For a long time most later works on the subject rested on it.

The original appeared in three editions, Florence 1612 and 1661 and Milan 1817. An English physician, Dr. Merret, turned it into Latin in 1662 with notes of his own, and Johann Kunckel published a revised German edition in 1689. A French version followed about a century later. The entry is frank about gaps in Neri's biography, yet clear on why his manual mattered to makers for generations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-strad:
Cremonese violin maker Antonio Stradivari, born in 1649 or 1650 and dead at Cremona in December 1737, built the instruments that still set the standard for string sound. No parish record of his birth survives at Cremona, so he was probably born in a nearby village. He began making stringed instruments in 1667, likely as a pupil in the workshop of Nicholas Amati, whose signed violins of that date may hide Stradivari's early hand.

In 1680 he set up on his own in the Piazza San Domenico and soon won fame. He improved Amati's model with better arching, more exact wood thickness, a changed scroll, and richer varnish. His finest instruments date from 1698 to 1725, when design, choice of wood, and finish reached their height. The entry follows a craftsman from workshop pupil to master whose name became shorthand for a perfect violin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bari:
Bari is an archdiocese in Apulia, southern Italy, its city the province's chief town on an Adriatic peninsula. Ancient Barium fell to Rome after the war with Pyrrhus yet kept its autonomy. As a seaport facing the East, it likely received Christianity very early, and tradition says St Peter preached there. Its first known bishop, Gervasius, attended Sardica in 347, and later bishops appear at Constantinople's orbit and Nicaea in 780.

Saracens wasted Apulia in the ninth century and seized Bari, but Byzantium retook it in 841. In 844 Angelarius of ruined Canosa brought relics of Rufinus, Memorus, and Sabinus to Bari, winning the double title Bari and Canosa. John XI granted the pallium in 933, and Giovanni II broke from Constantinople in 952. The diocese later counted 300,400 people, 33 parishes, 260 churches and chapels, and 250 secular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonaventura-c:
Bonaventura Cavalieri, an Italian mathematician and disciple of Galileo, gave geometry his Method of Indivisibles, a forerunner of integral calculus. Born at Milan in 1598, he joined the Jesuates at fifteen and studied under Castelli at Pisa. In 1629 he took the mathematics chair at Bologna, teaching there until his death in 1647 despite years of gout.

His Geometria of 1635 treats lines as endless points, surfaces as endless lines, and solids as endless surfaces, improving on the older Greek method. Pain from gout dogged him for years, and he turned to mathematics for relief, as Pascal had done. Guldinus attacked the idea as unsound, and Cavalieri answered in his Exercitationes Geometricae of 1647, which also first proved Pappus's theorem in full. He also spread the use of logarithms in Italy and wrote on conic sections, planets, and trigonometry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonizo-of-sut:
Bonizo of Sutri, an eleventh-century bishop and Gregorian partisan, chronicled his own age of pope against emperor. Born about 1045, probably at Cremona, he joined the Pataria reform party and clashed as subdeacon with the bishop of Piacenza. Gregory VII made him Bishop of Sutri in 1074, and he served as papal legate at Cremona in 1078.

Seized by Henry IV in 1082 and held by the antipope Clement III, he escaped after a year and sheltered with Countess Matilda of Tuscany. Elected to Piacenza in 1086, he took possession only in 1088 with Urban II's backing, and his enemies had him killed on 14 July 1090. His writings include the Decretum on church law and morals and the Liber ad amicum, a Church history from his own time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cagliari:
Cagliari, ancient Caralis, is the chief city and capital of Sardinia and a port on the Gulf of Cagliari. Carthaginians founded it, and Romans took it after the War of the Mercenaries. Vandals seized it in the fifth century, and Saracens held it in the eighth until Pisans helped expel them in 1022. Aragon took the city in 1324, and it stayed Spanish until 1714, passing in 1717 to the Duke of Savoy.

Its best known early bishop is Lucifer. From 354 to 371 he championed orthodoxy against Arianism as a friend of Saint Athanasius, yet late in life he authored a schism that bears his name. Under the Vandals, Sardinia sheltered Catholic bishops fleeing North Africa, among them Saints Eugenius and Fulgentius. Earlier bishops include Quintasius, present at Arles in 314, and Thomas and Januarius, named in Saint Gregory the Great's letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carbonari:
The Carbonari, or charcoal-burners, were a secret political society active chiefly in France and Italy in the early nineteenth century. Born from the political ferment of the French Revolution, the society first showed its power in Naples and the Papal States. Claims of an older origin, with Francis I of France as protector, are dismissed by the entry as improbable.

Members borrowed the charcoal trade's language for their secret life. The meeting place was a hut, its inner room a coal shop, and its surroundings a forest. Members called each other good cousin and outsiders heathens. Divided into apprentices and a higher grade, the society later declined, lingered briefly as a democratic Charbonnerie among French republicans until after 1841, and counted fewer members in Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathari:
Cathari, from the Greek word for pure, was a name given to several sects at different periods. Third-century Novatians and Manichaeans bore it, but it most often denotes the dualist sects of the later Middle Ages. They went by many other names as well. Some came from their trades, some from their leaders, and some from the towns where they gathered, including Albigenses from Albi.

The article sets out their dualist principles and then follows their history country by country: Italy, Germany and England, and the Balkan states. It closes by describing their relations with the Catholic Church. That account covers the preaching and inquisitorial campaigns mounted against them, and points readers to the sources for each region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chiavari:
On the Ligurian coast of northern Italy, the Diocese of Chiavari serves a city famed for fishing, slate, and cherrywood chairs. Chiavari stands on a small bay of the Gulf of Genoa and became a diocese in 1892, though the Archbishop of Genoa administered it until 1896. Its first bishop was Fortunato Vinelli, and its churches of the Madonna, Saint Francis, and Saint John grace the town.

Chiavari suffered after the Fieschi conspiracy of 1542, when its capture by the Counts of Lavagna left it suspected of siding with the plotters. Its notable citizens include Luca Cantiano di Moneglia, who founded a painting school, and Giuseppe Gregorio Solari, translator of Latin poets. The diocese counts 99,200 people, 138 parishes, 335 churches and chapels, and nearly 300 secular priests, with students, religious houses of men and women, and a busy commercial life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chytri:
An entry on Chytri, a titular see of Cyprus, beautifully placed in the island's centre, west of Messaria, in Chytraea's territory. The modern village of Kyrka, officially Kythraia in Greek, has kept the ancient name, and a pre-Phoenician necropolis has been found there. In Assurbanipal's day Pilagura ruled Kitrusi, one of ten Cypriot kingdoms, and many inscriptions in the Cypriot dialect survive.

Chytri was famed for worship of Apollo, Artemis, and Aphrodite Paphia, and its later names run Cythraia, Cythereia, Cythroi, and Chytrides. Cardinal Pelagius, papal legate, suppressed the Greek see of similar title in 1222. Lequien's list of bishops is very incomplete, with only eight recorded, from Saint Pappus, martyred under Licinius, Maximinus, or Constantius, to the most famous, Saint Demetrian, bishop from 885 to 912.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-pietro-:
A biographical entry introduces Count Pietro Verri, a Milanese economist born in 1728 and dead in 1797, whose theories sit midway between the Physiocrats and Adam Smith. After service in the Austrian army he turned to administration and political economy, rising to president of the Chamber of Accounts before retiring from public life in 1786.

With his brother Alessandro and the philosopher Beccaria he founded the Societa del Caffe, where philosophy, economy, and literature were debated. His chief works include Meditations on Political Economy and discourses on pleasure, pain, happiness, and the grain trade. His lasting merit, the entry argues, is his clear statement of the theory of demand and supply, defended in controversy with Melchiorre Gioia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-vittori:
This biographical entry presents Count Vittorio Alfieri, called the greatest tragic poet of Italy. He was born at Asti in 1749 and died at Florence in 1803. After fruitless schooling at Turin's Royal Academy, he spent years in restless travel, gambling, and intrigue across Europe. Near his twenty-ninth year his genius awoke, driving him to master Italian, Latin, and finally Greek.

Italy had no tragic drama worthy of the name until Alfieri created it. Settling at Florence in 1778, he wrote the tragedies that made his fame. His later life was bound to Louisa von Stolberg-Gedern, Countess of Albany, wife of the Stuart Pretender. After the Pretender's death he lived with her unwedded. His religious feeling, the entry insists, remained strong and sincere to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dante-alighie:
A biographical entry presents Dante Alighieri, Italy's supreme poet, born at Florence in 1265 and dead at Ravenna in 1321. His own words in Paradiso place his birth between 18 May and 17 June, when the sun stood in Gemini. Son of a notary from an ancient but fading Guelph family, he grew up amid Florence's democratic triumphs and fought in the Guelph cavalry at Campaldino in 1289.

Enrolled in the guild of physicians and apothecaries to hold office, he spoke in the commune's council in 1295 and served the republic before exile in 1302. The entry follows his love for Beatrice, his political ruin, and his writing of the Divine Comedy, the Convivio, and De Monarchia. It closes with Dante societies at Cambridge, Oxford, and London keeping his scholarship alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenichino-d:
Domenichino, properly Domenico Zampieri, was an Italian painter born at Bologna on 21 October 1581. He began under Calvaert, but ill treatment there led his father, a poor shoemaker, to place him in the Carracci Academy. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his slow, thoughtful ways won him the nickname of the Ox, shared with his master Ludovico. He took the academy's prize for drawing, gaining fame and hatred together.

He studied the human face until Bellori said he could delineate the soul, then visited Parma and Rome. At Rome his patron Cardinal Agucchi opened doors, and his works reached the Louvre, the National Gallery, and the Hermitage. He died at Naples in 1641, a painter of patience and deep feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-palm:
Domenico Palmieri was a theologian born at Piacenza on 4 July 1829 who died at Rome in 1909. He was ordained in 1852 and entered the Society of Jesus the same year. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his teaching of rhetoric, philosophy, theology, and Scripture, above all during sixteen years as professor at the Roman College. There he won fame as a philosopher.

His Institutions of Philosophy, three volumes from 1874 to 1876, kept the scholastic method yet broke with common Peripatetic views, above all on the makeup of bodies. Later he turned his learning to Dante, writing a work praised for its learned introduction and notes on each canto. The entry presents a thinker of depth in two fields at once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaudenzio-fer:
Gaudenzio Ferrari, the greatest master of the Piedmontese school, painted sacred stories for the people of north Italy. Born at Valduggia around 1470, he worked almost wholly in Piedmont and Lombardy, learning expression from Leonardo at Milan and architecture from Bramante's circle. His earliest known works date from 1508 and 1511, when he was already forty.

Ferrari stands alone among Italian Renaissance painters as a truly religious master, never bowing to pagan fashion. He painted long sacred dramas for churches alone: a Passion at Varallo, lives of the Virgin and Magdalene at Vercelli, grouped at times like mystery plays. German feeling runs through his naturalistic art, and he died at Milan in January 1546.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giorgio-vasar:
Giorgio Vasari was a painter, architect, and writer born at Arezzo in 1511, who died at Florence in 1574. Though an artist of repute, he owes his lasting fame to his Lives of the most eminent painters, sculptors, and architects.
