A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls that huge work the treasure-house to which all later writers on early Italian art have gone.

First published at Florence in 1550, the Lives is uneven, since prejudice colors some portraits. On the whole it stands as a marvel of good writing and accuracy. Later editors, above all Milanesi in 1868, added notes and fresh material. Vasari's own paintings and his letters and Ragionamenti fill out the picture of a man trained under Michelangelo who knew the great age firsthand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-barb:
Giovanni Barbieri, called Il Guercino from his squint, was a famous painter of religious subjects. He was born at Cento near Bologna in 1591, and died at Bologna in 1666. His parents were poor, yet before he was ten he had painted a Virgin on the front wall of his home. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him from a youth admiring Carracci to a master with his own academy.

Trained under Bertozzi and Gennari at Cento, he won protection from Father Mirandola and commissions through his talent. At Rome, Cardinal Ludovisi, later Gregory XV, drew him to paint the Aurora at the Villa Ludovisi and St. Petronilla in the Capitol. Refusing invitations from James I and Louis XIII to go to England and to visit France, he returned to Cento and founded a much-frequented academy. After Guido's death he settled at Bologna, leaving much wealth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregorio-alle:
Gregorio Allegri was a composer and priest born at Rome about 1580, who died in 1652. Attached to the cathedral at Fermo as a beneficiary priest, he acted as chorister and composer. Pope Urban VIII, drawn by his motets and concerti, appointed him to the Papal Choir on 6 December 1629. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a man of priestly piety and humility.

His fame climaxed in the nine-voiced Miserere for two choirs. Its value depends almost entirely on its execution, above all old ornaments that give many passages a strange, sad quality. Without them the piece appears almost lifeless. His published works are chiefly two volumes of Concertini of 1618 to 1619 and two of motetti of 1621, while many manuscripts survive in Roman archives and libraries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-von-v:
Hermann von Vicari was archbishop of Freiburg in Baden, born at Aulendorf in 1773 and dead at Freiburg in 1868. After study in law and theology he was ordained in 1797, served the curia at Constance, and rose through canon, vicar-general, and dean to archbishop in 1842. His long life spanned the upheavals that reshaped the German church after the old dioceses were suppressed.

As archbishop he fought to free the church in Baden from state control and from Josephinism, the system that put church affairs under civil rule. He defended bishops' rights over clergy training and appointments, enforced discipline on mixed marriages, and even endured police watch and confinement in his palace. He founded a boys' seminary from his own funds and rebuilt Catholic life in Baden with stubborn resolve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-honore-fabri:
Honoré Fabri, also called Lefèvre, was a Jesuit theologian born about 1607 in the French department of Ain and dead at Rome in 1688. Avignon saw him join the Society of Jesus in 1626, and mental work filled his life thereafter. Mathematics and physics were his strongest fields, though controversy also made him formidable.

At Lyons' Jesuit college he taught philosophy for eight years and mathematics for six, winning many pupils through his learning. Called to Rome, he served thirty years as theologian to the papal penitentiary at the Vatican basilica. Sommervogel lists thirty-one published works under his name, plus fourteen manuscripts at Lyons, including his 1659 dialogue on probable opinion, attacked by Stephanus Gradius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-janos-zadori:
Church writer János Zádori, also called Drexler, was born at Katloez, Neutra County, Hungary, on 6 March 1831. He died at Gran on 30 December 1887. He studied at Vienna university's Pazmaneum. His favorite branches were modern languages, literature, and natural sciences. Ordained priest in December 1854, he served as chaplain at Balassa-Gyarmat for ten years, then from 1864 until life's end taught dogmatic theology at Gran's archiepiscopal seminary.

Honors came as member of the metropolitan chapter and domestic prelate of Leo XIII, while appointment to the Neusohl see he declined. Thirty-eight of his works appeared in print, among them devotional pieces and memorial sermons, one on Count Stephen Széchenyi. His principal work, A társadalom alapelvei, or Fundamental Principles of Human Society, appeared at Budapest in 1864, developing Lacordaire's ideas against modern errors, a Hungarian seminary professor of wide output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-moreri:
Louis Moreri was a French encyclopaedist, born at Bargemont in 1643 and dead at Paris in 1680. His grandfather had taken the name Moreri from a Provencal village, and Louis studied at Draguignan, Aix, and Lyons, preaching five years in Lyons after ordination.

There he dreamed up a dictionary holding all the notable facts of sacred and profane history and myth. Le Grand Dictionnaire historique appeared at Lyons in 1671, flawed yet useful, and later Paris and Amsterdam editions improved it greatly, the twentieth and last being the best. Bayle, who planned to mend its gaps, praised the pioneer compiler's labour and service to all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucifer-of-ca:
Lucifer of Cagliari was a fourth-century Sardinian bishop, born early in the century and dead in 371. He first appears in 354, sent by Pope Liberius with Pancratius and Hilary to ask Constantius for a council on Athanasius and his condemnation.

At Milan he defended Alexandria's bishop with passion and harsh words, giving foes a pretext for fresh condemnation, and Constantius exiled him to Syria, Palestine, and the Thebaid. There he penned a fiery defence of orthodoxy that overshot its mark. Freed under Julian, he went to Antioch and worsened its split by consecrating a rival bishop and pressing hard on waverers from Nicaea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-antonio:
Luigi Antonio Muratori was a Modenese library keeper and one of his age's greatest scholars, born at Vignola in 1672 and dead in 1750. Poor-born, he studied law, philosophy, and theology at Modena, was ordained in 1694, and joined Milan's Ambrosian Library scholars in 1695.

There he began harvesting old writings never yet printed, starting with Latin Anecdota in 1697. Duke Rinaldo made him Modena's keeper of records and books in 1700, a post he held to his death, adding a parish post in 1716. His Este old records defended his duke against Rome over Comacchio, and his vast Rerum Italicarum Scriptores gathered Italy's medieval chronicles for all later historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-palmier:
Luigi Palmieri was an Italian physicist and meteorologist, born at Faicchio in 1807 and dead at Naples in 1896. After Caiazzo seminary he studied mathematics and science at Naples, took an architecture degree, and taught at Salerno, Campobasso, and Avellino.

Professor of physics at Naples naval school in 1845 and at the university in 1847, he joined the Vesuvius observatory in 1848 and directed it from 1854. He watched every eruption, nearly dying in 1872, and built delicate tools. A tuned electrometer tracked air electricity over forty years. A seismometer sensed faint tremors and foretold eruptions, and a telegraph variant, anemometer, and rain gauge joined his inventions. Senator and Lincei member, he held faith as his studies' guide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-macri:
Macri, or Macras, is a titular see in Mauretania Sitifiensis, appearing only in the Notitia Africae and the Antonine Itinerary. It flourished long and drew praise from Arabian writers, lying south-west of Setif, in the plain of Bou Megueur, on the Oued-Magra, which still keeps its name, near Djebel Magra.

In 411 Macri had a Donatist bishop, Maximus, at the Carthage Conference. In 479 Huneric banished many Catholics from the town and desert regions, and in 484 Emeritus, Bishop of Macri, sat at the Carthage Assembly and shared the same banishment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missouri:
Missouri was carved out of the Louisiana Territory and takes its name from the river flowing through its centre, a name meaning big muddy in the Indian language. Geographically it is the central commonwealth of the Federal Union, bounded by Iowa, Arkansas, Illinois, Kentucky, Tennessee, Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma. North of the Missouri River lie rolling prairies, while the south holds the Ozark uplands.

The state is divided into three dioceses, St. Louis in the east, Kansas City in the west south of the Missouri, and St. Joseph in the west north of the river. In 1909 its Catholic population was 452,703, including about 3,000 Catholic negroes. Church property is exempt from taxation up to one acre in cities and five acres beyond them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-muri:
Muri, now Muri-Gries, is a Benedictine abbey that flourished for over eight centuries at Muri near Basle in Switzerland. It now stands under Austrian rule at Gries near Bozen in Tyrol. The monastery of Saint Martin at Muri was founded in 1027 by the illustrious house of Habsburg. Its lands were given by the Habsburg founders with Werner, Bishop of Strasbourg.

Monks from Einsiedeln under Prior Reginbold peopled the new house, and Burchard became its first abbot in 1055. He consecrated the abbey church in 1064, long the burial place of the Habsburg dynasty. A colony from Saint Blaise in the Black Forest reinforced it. Through the Middle Ages it pursued quiet work of religion and civilisation under able abbots, until modern upheavals moved it to Gries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nepi-and-sutr:
Nepi and Sutri are united sees of the province of Rome, in the Ciminian region of central Italy. Nepi stands on a tufa hill ringed by great walls. Its cathedral, on the site of an ancient temple of Jupiter, holds paintings by Titian, Perugino and Zuccari. Vignola began its communal palace, and Peter Louis Farnese built its fort. Ruins of an amphitheatre and ancient baths remain, source of Vatican statues including a basalt King Nectanebo I.

Nepete and Sutrium belonged to the Faliscans, who called Rome against Etruscan invaders, and Livy calls them the gates of Etruria. They became Latin colonies in 382. In the Gothic War Nepi was among the Goths' last strongholds, and Lombards sacked it in 569. In the eighth century it housed Tuto, a Lombard duke known for meddling in the papal election of 768. The entry follows both sees through imperial-papal struggles to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-speda:
Sicilian priest and philosopher Nicolas Spedalieri defended Christian faith against the Enlightenment from Rome. Born at Bronte in 1740, he studied at Monreale, taught philosophy, mathematics, and theology, and cultivated poetry, music, and painting beside his priestly work.

Driven from Monreale by a storm over his theses, he lived ten lean years in Rome before Pius VI gave him a Vatican benefice in 1784. His books answer Fréret and Gibbon, argue that Christian religion aids civil society, and treat the art of governing. He died in 1795. For ten years in Rome he lived in penury while studying and writing fruitfully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostia-and-vel:
Ostia and Velletri form a suburbicarian diocese near Rome, headed by the ancient port of Rome. Ostia, first colony of Ancus Marcius, grew on salt trade, and Claudius built it an artificial harbour, which Trajan enlarged with a basin and canal. A new city, Portus Romanus, rose beside it, graced by emperors and joined to Rome by the Via Portuensis.

With the empire's fall both towns decayed, and by the tenth century the harbour basin was marsh. Gregory IV refounded the city as Gregoriopolis, Leo IV beat the Saracen fleet off Ostia in 847, and later popes and cardinals refortified it. Excavations begun under Pius VII bared the forum, a theatre, three temples, shrines of Mithra and the Great Mother, the emporium, and many inscriptions. Velletri's bishops and churches close the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-caliari:
Paolo Caliari, also called Paolo Veronese, was a leading painter of the Venetian school, born at Verona in 1528 and dead at Venice on 19 April 1588. Son of the sculptor Gabriele Caliari, he first learned his father's craft, then turned to painting under Antonio Badile of Verona. Early works followed at Verona, Mantua, and Castelfranco, where he frescoed the Villa Soranzo.

Summoned to Venice in 1555, he painted the ceiling of San Sebastiano to such praise that more work in the church followed. Titian chose him in 1561 for the Library of Saint Mark, where his three medallions won the gold chain for the best painting. In 1562 he painted the Marriage at Cana for San Giorgio Maggiore, now in the Louvre, and further great feast scenes followed, with superb wall pieces on Saint Sebastian's martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penne-and-atr:
Penne and Atri were two ancient Italian towns joined as a single diocese in 1152. Penne, the Pinna of the Vestini, stayed loyal to Rome through the Marsic War. Sulla later wrecked it, the Lombard Duchy of Benevento held it, and Saracens sacked it in the ninth century. Atri, the Hadria of the Piceni, became a Roman colony around 282 BC, and its old walls still stood. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry covers both towns and their shared see.

Legend made Patrassus, one of the seventy disciples, Penne's first bishop, and St. Maximus is honoured at its cathedral. Atri's cathedral, a fine Italian Gothic building with a campanile near 200 feet high, anchors the other half. The entry runs through the united bishops, from Beroaldo through the imprisoned Cistercian Nicolo and the deposed Tommaso Consuberi, and counts 95 parishes and over 180,000 souls in the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrus-boeri:
Petrus Boeri was a French Benedictine canonist and bishop of the Great Schism, born early in the fourteenth century at Laredorte. First mentioned in 1350 as Abbot of St. Chinian, he won Urban V's favour by virtue and learning and became Bishop of Orvieto in 1364, then of Vaison near Avignon in 1370. Within a year of Urban's death he returned to Orvieto and held it until 1379.

The Schism undid him twice. Urban VI stripped him of Orvieto in 1379 for backing the Avignon antipope Robert of Geneva, and Clement VII himself deposed him in 1387, handing Orvieto's care to the Bishop of Grasse. Between depositions he served Charles V of France as ambassador to the Avignon court. He died probably in 1388, leaving two commentaries on St. Benedict's Rule, one canonist's, one ascetic's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-alfier:
Pietro Alfieri was a Roman priest and musician who preserved sixteenth-century church music for later singers. He was born at Rome in 1801 and once a Camaldolese monk. He taught singing for many years at the English College in Rome and gathered the old masters' music into scholarly collections.

His seven-volume Collection of Sacred Music reprinted chiefly Palestrina, and he added smaller sets of motets and excerpts from writers on music. On plainchant, the unaccompanied chant of the liturgy, he published studies of organ accompaniment and the restoration of Gregorian songbooks. He also wrote a history of Gregorian chant and translated a French treatise on harmony.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quam-singular:
Quam Singulari is a decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Sacraments, dated 8 August 1910, on the age for first Communion. It was promulgated on 15 August 1910. This encyclopedia entry stresses that the decree starts no new discipline. It brings back the Church's ancient, universal law wherever it had lapsed. The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 had already bound all who reach the years of discretion to receive Communion, and that canon was never revoked.

Giving Communion to infants just after baptism was an old custom, changed over time but never condemned, and still approved among Greeks and Orientals. What must a child know? Not memorized theological definitions, which may mean nothing to a young mind. The child must tell Eucharistic bread from common bread, knowing that what looks like bread holds the real Body and Blood of Christ. Grace, good intention and fasting complete the preparation the decree requires.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-alexis-:
Alexis Falconieri was born in Florence in 1200 and died at Mount Senario in 1310. Son of Bernard Falconieri, a merchant prince of Florence, he grew up humble. Alexis joined the Laudesi, a confraternity of the Blessed Virgin, meeting there his six future companions. Favoured with an apparition of the Mother of God on 15 August 1233, the seven soon founded the Servite Order.

Alexis at once abandoned all, retiring to La Camarzia, then to Mount Senario. In humility he begged alms for his brethren through his city's streets. Though living to 110 years, he refused the priesthood, deeming himself unworthy. In 1252 the new Cafaggio church was completed under his care. In a few years ten thousand enrolled in the Servite Order. At his death the Infant Jesus visited him visibly. Clement XI declared him worthy of veneration in 1717.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-joseph-:
Saint Joseph, Missouri, began as a trading post of Joseph Robidoux, a Catholic who in 1830 became sole owner of the post at Roy's Branch above the Blacksnake Hills. An itinerant Jesuit said Mass in Robidoux's log house in 1838, and Father Vogel served the faithful from 1840. Robidoux had Fred Smith survey the town, and Smith's plat, named Saint Joseph, was recorded at Saint Louis on 26 July 1843.

Thomas Scanlon, the first permanent pastor, began work in 1847, and a brick church begun that June was dedicated in September by Archbishop Kenrick of Saint Louis. The California rush of 1849 made Saint Joseph a leading starting point, with about 1900 people. Proposed as a see in 1866, it gained its first bishop, John Hogan, in 1868, when some 3000 souls were served by five priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-louis-m:
Saint Louis became a diocese on 2 July 1826 and an archdiocese on 20 July 1847. It covers 26,235 square miles of Missouri, bounded by the Mississippi on the east and Arkansas on the south. The city was founded in 1764 by Pierre Laclède, a French nobleman who had come to Louisiana in 1755 and entered trade in New Orleans.

After the Treaty of Paris ended his firm's Indian-trade privilege in 1763, he left Fort Chartres. He landed on the Mississippi's west bank and laid out Saint Louis in what was then wilderness. At first the young city belonged to the diocese of Santiago de Cuba, since Spain did not formally occupy Louisiana until 1770. Only two priests served the territory, the Recollect Luke Collet and the Jesuit Meurin, and Collet's death in 1765 left Meurin alone in the valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sassari:
Sassari, an archdiocese in Sardinia on the Rossello river in a fertile land of oil, fruit, wine, and tobacco, holds a university founded in 1634. Its cathedral keeps a monument to the Duke of Maurienne, and the Trinity church holds a fine fifteenth-century picture by an unknown hand. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a city that rose as Torres fell.

Unknown until about the eleventh century, Sassari grew as ancient Torres decayed. Genoese sacked it in 1166. In 1291 it became a republic with Genoese consent, glad to see it slip from Pisan control. Its statutes of 1316 stand out for mild penalties beside the harsh laws of the age. In 1390 it joined the giudicato of Arborea, and the entry follows its later fortunes under Aragon and Savoy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scutari:
Scutari's first known bishop is Bassus in 387. The see began under Salonica, primate of all Illyricum, then passed to Achrida when Justinian moved the primacy there. In the early Middle Ages it answered to Dioclea. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows an Albanian see through centuries of silence and martyrdom.

From the seventh to the mid-twelfth century no bishop is known. Among later bishops stand Francis II de Sanctis and Dominicus Andrijasevic, theologian and philosopher who died at Rome in 1639. Andrijasevic befriended Gregory XV and Urban VIII. Dominicus Babic and Antonius de Nigris, martyred by Turks in 1702, also stand out. In 1867 Pius IX joined Scutari principally with Antivari, making it an archdiocese and metropolis under Charles Pooten, who died at Scutari in 1886. Only fifty-three bishops are known from 1063 to 1886.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-solari:
The Solari were a family of Milanese artists whose work shaped the city's cathedral and the Certosa monastery near Pavia in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces several generations of the clan, from builders who raised churches and fortifications to painters trained in Venice and Milan.

Guiniforte Solari helped design the Certosa and the Sforza castle, while his son Pietro Antonio later carried the family's craft to Moscow, where he worked on rebuilding the Kremlin. Andrea Solari, trained under Giovanni Bellini, absorbed Leonardo da Vinci's manner so closely that he passed for Leonardo's finest pupil, and his later pictures glow with clear, bright colour. Works in Milan, Paris, and London anchor the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alphonsus-:
St. Alphonsus Liguori, born at Marianella near Naples on 27 September 1696 and dead at Nocera de' Pagani on 1 August 1787. He was one of the eighteenth century's three great missionaries, beside Leonard of Port Maurice and Paul of the Cross. This very long entry follows a child of an old but impoverished noble house. He was son of Don Joseph, captain of the royal galleys, and a mother of Spanish descent, baptized two days after birth in Naples.

From prodigy to lawyer to priest, Alphonsus founded the Redemptorists, wrote moral theology that shaped confessors for generations, and endured the trials of his order with patience. Readers get a full life of a saint whose books and missions remade popular preaching in southern Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-juliana-fa:
Juliana Falconieri, foundress of the Servite Sisters, took the Third Order habit about 1285 and kept its rule at home. Born in 1270 to Florence's noble Falconieri family, she was niece of Alexis Falconieri, one of the Servites' seven founders. Through his influence she consecrated herself from earliest youth to religious life and Christian perfection. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 12 June 1341.

After her father's death she received the Third Order habit from Philip Benitius, then Servite general. Until her mother's death she stayed in her parents' house, following Philip's rule in perfect chastity, strict mortification, severe penance, zealous prayer, and charity. After her mother died, she and companions moved in 1305 into their own house, the first convent of Servite Third Order Sisters, with Juliana as superior for life. Their dress was a black gown, leather girdle, and white veil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-philip-rom:
Philip Neri, the apostle of Rome, turned joy, music, and friendship into an instrument of reform. Born at Florence on 22 July 1515 to the notary Francesco Neri, he grew up among Dominicans of San Marco, steeped in Savonarola's memory. As a boy he was called the good Pippo, fond of reciting psalms with his sisters.

In Rome he lived as a layman on bread, water, and herbs, prayed long vigils in the catacombs, and gathered disciples who formed the Brotherhood of the Little Oratory. In 1548 he founded a confraternity with his confessor Persiano Rosa. Ordained late, he preached with humour and warmth, heard confessions for hours, and died on 27 May 1595. The entry captures a saint of laughter and charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-oratory-o:
Communities following Philip Neri's rule, in Italy, Spain, England, and beyond, are gathered here. The sixteenth-century revolt, threatening the Church's very life, drew out a marvellous fruitfulness: Jesuits under Ignatius, Theatines under Cajetan, Barnabites under Zaccaria, Hospitallers under John of God, and Philip's Oratory. Disciples first met at San Girolamo in Rome for spiritual instruction.

Philip, now a priest, built an oratory over an aisle of San Girolamo, giving the congregation its name. In 1564 he took charge of the Florentines' church, where priest disciples said Mass and preached four sermons daily amid hymns and popular devotions. Growth, houses, and the Oratory's gentle spirit fill the rest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ubanghi-chari:
Ubangi-Chari was a prefecture apostolic in Equatorial Africa, carved out of the older vicariate of Ubangi in May 1909. A prefecture apostolic is a mission district below a diocese in rank. It lay west of the Bahr-el-Ghazal country and south of the Chad district, stretching across a wide belt of savanna and river country. Its first mission post had been planted at Sainte-Famille on the Upper Ubangi in 1895, among the Banziri people, in land then almost unknown.

The entry records the prefecture's founding at the request of Bishop Augouard. It was placed under the Fathers of the Holy Ghost, and Father Pierre Catel was named its first prefect apostolic, resident at Sainte-Famille. It lists its stations, priests, and people reached in its early years. The result is a snapshot of a young mission field on the edge of French Equatorial Africa, still taking shape.
doe-osti-17019158-faster-simulation-code:
Faster simulation is the goal of this abbreviated final report from Lawrence Livermore, dated September 2026. Rui Peng Li, Socratis Petrides, Kowshik Thopalli, and Jin Yao combined machine learning with algebraic multigrid. That method is a leading solver for the huge linear equation systems that eat most run time in physics codes. Tuning it by hand for each new problem is hard.

The team taught software to learn coarse level operators, smoothing steps, and coarse variable choices, and built a shared test environment called AMGLearn. In sample tests, learned coarse operators cut coarse level complexity by at least 44 percent without hurting solver strength. A side study also cut error in a mesh free shock wave method by tuning its kernel and starting layout.
doe-osti-17038130-rapid-fabrication-of-s:
Alexander Baker of Lawrence Livermore reports in September 2026 on making solid state batteries by cold spray. Cold spray is a coating method that fires tiny particles in fast gas so they stick and build a dense layer. Solid state batteries promise higher capacity and better safety for vehicles, but costly making and weak layer contact have held them back.

The project sprayed thin cathode layers from a nickel manganese cobalt oxide, called NMC 622, and electrolyte layers from a lithium indium chloride. Mixed composite cathodes were also sprayed, with no solvent used at any stage. Sprayed cathodes kept the electrochemical behavior of tape cast samples. A partner model at UC Davis captured how binders and surface roughness affect particle sticking.
doe-osti-17076228-fy26-end-of-year-repor:
End of year fiscal 2026 report ORNL/SPR-2026/4946, by David Guenaga, Omar Marcillo, Monica Maceira, and James Garner of Oak Ridge, tracks a seismic watch system for underground sites. The goal is spotting odd vibration signals that could hint at containment breaches or other safeguard relevant activity at geological storage sites. Sensors combine surface seismometers with fiber optic acoustic sensing underground.

Work built on a waveform database and a ground truth event catalog set up in fiscal 2025. A new workflow hunts narrow band signals, the kind made by generators, pumps, and ventilation gear, by stacking spectrograms across stations and stripping broadband noise. Peak picking and tracking tools then follow those signals over time and frequency.
doe-osti-17084191-mesoscopic-modelling-o:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-26681R, printed September 2026, sums up modeling work on nonlinear optical materials by Alexander Cerjan, Weng Chow, and Christopher Moore. Light can drive such materials into fast changing states that plain steady models miss. Three linked efforts share that theme of coupled light, material, and feedback behavior.

One effort modeled laser triggered vacuum switches, where a light pulse starts electron emission, vaporization, and breakdown across a high voltage gap. A second studied frequency combs in exceptional point lasers, including states that split and double in period. A third applied quasinormal coupled mode analysis to structured optical systems. Each part aims at models fast enough to guide real device design.
doe-osti-17120057-scalable-inductionless:
YuHsiang Lan, Khanh Nguyen, Paul Fischer, and colleagues at Argonne add magnetohydrodynamics to the NekRS flow code and prove it out in report ANL-26/45. The target is the fusion blanket, where liquid metal coolant flows through strong magnetic fields. Their version is inductionless, treating the field as imposed rather than solved, which suits slow conducting flows.

Chapters set out the governing equations, the weak form used for discretization, and boundary treatment at walls and interfaces. Four test problems check the code: Hartmann flow, the Hunt II duct case, a pipe under a fringing field, and a linear stability case. A performance chapter then measures how the solver scales, ahead of a short conclusion on readiness.
doe-osti-17185621-measurements-of-a-grow:
Brianna Matthews, Brian Viner, Dalton Hare, and Savannah River colleagues measured weather around a growing season prescribed burn, in report SRNL-STI-2026-00579 dated September 2026. The Forest Service burns tracts at the Savannah River Site to cut wildfire risk and keep timber and habitat healthy. Each managed burn is also a chance to record how fire and weather interact.

The burn took place on 4 June 2026 near Mona Bay, one of the shallow Carolina bay wetlands on site. Three portable weather stations at 3 meters logged wind speed and direction, temperature, humidity, pressure, and rain. Drone flights added profiles above the surface. Data feed the QUIC-Fire spread model and pair with a dormant season burn measured in February for contrast.
doe-osti-2589382-sup-129-sup-i-sup-99-su:
Katie Hill, Daniel Kaplan, and Kimberly Roberts measure how strongly three risky nuclides stick to soil at a planned Oak Ridge waste site, in Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2021-00404. The site is the proposed Environmental Management Disposal Facility on the Oak Ridge Reservation. The measured values, called distribution coefficients, feed safety calculations for the burial ground.

Fourteen geological materials from the site were tested in batch sorption runs. Iodine-129 bound weakly to moderately, averaging 37.8 milliliters per gram, about ten times the value used in earlier safety runs. Technetium-99 bound far more strongly than expected, with a median of 365.7 milliliters per gram. Five materials grabbed so much that the soluble form likely changed into a form that barely dissolves. Uranium results complete the set planners need.
doe-osti-2998402-flexible-pilot-jobs-fra:
Fermilab report FERMILAB-TM-2895-STUDENT, by Franco Terranova under Marco Mambelli's supervision, comes from the laboratory's Italian summer school in scientific computing. The subject is GlideinWMS, the workload system that farms particle physics jobs out to computers worldwide. Its pilot jobs land on a remote machine first, then pull real work matched to that machine's capacity.

The framework study weighs new flexibility for what a pilot may carry. One proposal adds web files as a job input type: a glidein could start a small web server and serve custom dashboards for watching a job run. Example markup in the report shows how a user would declare such files. The project sits inside the computing stack that experiments such as CMS and DUNE depend on to process the largest data sets in science.
doe-osti-2999103-beyond-magic-barrels-di:
Rekha Rao, Helen Cleaves, Tyler Kennelly and a Sandia team, with partners at Purdue and Florida State, report in SAND2025-12370R, printed September 2025, on digital manufacturing for crystallisation. Making explosive materials means growing crystals of set size and shape. Yet recipes are often found by trial in what the title calls magic barrels. This second part uses resveratrol, a compound that forms needle like crystals, as a stand in for explosives.

The team attacked the problem at several scales at once. Microscopy tracked crystal growth over time. Bench reactors grew thousands of crystals, checked by microscopy and X ray tomography. Models ranged from atom level theory to kinetic Monte Carlo codes, plus population balance equations for well mixed tanks. Against an EasyMax reactor run with 5 percent seed, fast and slow cooling, the model captured the main trends. A follow on project continues the work.
doe-osti-3007587-small-scale-melter-test:
Vitreous State Laboratory report VSL-07R1220-1, Revision 0, by K. S. Matlack, I. L. Pegg, W. Gong, W. Kot, and co-workers at the Catholic University of America, documents small-scale melter tests of high-level waste glasses. The glasses were not chosen one by one: an algorithm generated the candidate formulas, and Matrix 1 was the first test set.

Run tables record each glass batch melted, with dates, compositions, and measured properties such as viscosity and electrical conductivity at temperature. The work supports the Hanford vitrification program, where radioactive tank waste will be locked into glass logs. Long data tables fill much of the report, giving the raw record behind later glass-formulation decisions.
doe-osti-3007692-interactions-between-cl:
Final report for DOE award DE-SC0022047, by Ian Williams of Iowa State University with co-investigator William Gallus, examines how clouds and wind-driven surface heat exchanges interact over land. The evidence mixes Atmospheric Radiation Measurement observations with experiments in the E3SM Earth system model.

At 3 kilometre resolution, boundary layer rolls and cells stamped coherent patterns of about 50 watts per square metre onto surface heat fluxes. The team also found models overestimate wind shear inside convective cold pools, a bias that distorts gusts. Fluxes and updraft scales proved linked in a multivariate way, which explains why a single stability number predicted them poorly. The findings feed better flux and gust formulas for storm prediction.
doe-osti-3011272-survey-of-neutron-induc:
Neutron induced fission data for four actinides are surveyed by Sieverding, Tonchev, and Quaglioni of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in LLNL-TR-2011748. The review covers uranium 233, plutonium 238, plutonium 240, and plutonium 242 for incident neutrons from 100 keV to 20 MeV. Experimental results are compared against the ENDF/B-VIII.1, JENDL-5, and JEFF-3.3 libraries and LLNL's own ENDL-2009.5.

For plutonium 238, few and discrepant data above 6 MeV leave relative uncertainties near 20 percent in JENDL-5 and JEFF-3.3 above 10 MeV, while ENDF/B-VIII.1 stays under 10 percent. The survey closes each isotope section with a recommendation on which library to use.
doe-osti-3012388-carbon-capture-plant-fr:
A front end engineering design study for carbon capture at a cement plant is delivered under cooperative agreement DE-FE0032220, with Vijay Gupta as principal investigator. Cemex hosts the application, SLB partners on the work, and RTI contributors staff much of the engineering team. The January 2026 report assembles the design package for the capture plant.

Contents run from process overview and host site integration to schedule and site arrangement. Design philosophies govern details such as compressor discharge piping, which is rated to the highest potential discharge pressure of each stage. Integration challenges between the capture unit and cement operations receive dedicated treatment in the study.
doe-osti-3014070-depletion-benchmark-of-:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/EXT-21-01568, by Joseph Nielsen and Brittany Grayson, dated February 2025, builds a depletion benchmark from the AFIP-7 experiment in the Advanced Test Reactor. Benchmarks for how low-enriched uranium fuel burns down over time are scarce, especially for uranium-10 percent molybdenum plate fuel. That alloy is the candidate fuel for converting U.S. high-performance research reactors away from highly enriched uranium.

AFIP-7 placed a full-size fuel plate in the reactor's center flux trap, position 7. The report assembles the experiment model, including hafnium control components and reflector compositions, and computes eigenvalues for operating cycles 149B and 150B. Other institutions can now test their reactor physics codes against the same documented irradiation instead of relying on proprietary data.
doe-osti-3014985-lahaina-energy-partners:
Rebuilding Lahaina's energy system after the fire is the subject of a June 2025 slide deck from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and Lahaina's local partners. The partnership is community-led: Lāhainā Strong, Hā Sustainability, and Shake Energy Collaborative convene residents to name energy priorities, while the national lab runs analysis to support local decisions. Robin Burton headed the presenter list.

The technical assistance plan runs about seventeen months across building modeling, microgrids, and distribution grid work. Early tasks map resilience hubs and review policy and business model options. Middle tasks compare microgrid costs and benefits at priority sites, then build cost-optimized designs for two sites with one-line diagrams and cost estimates. A final implementation guide covers home and business scale microgrids, including siting and sizing, so residents can act on the findings.
doe-osti-3017160-challenges-and-opportun:
Stuart M Cohen, Nathalie Voisin, Thushara De Silva, Todd Levin, Ningchao Gao, Patrick Balducci, and Brenda Pracheil wrote this February 2026 report, NLR/TP-6A40-93309. It examines how electric utilities model and value new assets, using pumped storage hydropower as the case study. Pumped storage moves water uphill when power is cheap, then releases it for power when demand peaks.

The review walks through four model families: capacity expansion, production cost, hydrological systems, and transmission reliability. It then asks how well they connect. Transmission plans, for example, feed reliability models that judge pumped storage alongside other assets. The authors find the seams between models are where valuation goes wrong. In a future grid heavy with variable renewables and inverter-based resources, those seams decide real investments. Utilities and regulators get a map of what to fix.
doe-osti-3017544-analyzing-scm-grid-bene:
Jesse Bennett and Mingzhi Zhang presented these slides on September 17, 2025, to the US Drive grid integration tech team. The topic is smart charge management for electric vehicles: shifting when vehicles charge so the grid benefits instead of straining. Their EV-CENTS project builds the financial framework for judging that value, through two new metrics.

One metric is the cost of electricity for charging; the other is an annual cost of charging per vehicle. Both cover home, depot, workplace, street, and public fast charging. A co-simulation study ran 72 hours at fifteen-minute intervals across 58 feeders in Richmond and Newport News, Virginia. Vehicle mixes included personal cars, transit and school buses, and freight trucks, at roughly fifty percent adoption. Feeder loading rose substantially where many vehicles plugged in. Utilities get numbers for when managed charging pays for itself.
doe-osti-3022114-computational-design-to:
ORNL report ORNL/TM-2026/4443 is the final report for CRADA NFE-24-10252 with Carpenter Technology Corporation. It describes a computational route to qualifying a high gamma-prime alloy for additively manufactured turbine parts. Raising turbine inlet heat improves engine efficiency. Laser powder bed fusion can build the intricate internal cooling passages of parts like tip shoes. But new alloys often crack during stress relief or hot isostatic pressing.

The team built a physics-informed model of the process for Carpenter's GammaPrint-1100 alloy. Melt-pool dimensions tuned the model. Deflections after wire-EDM cutting validated its residual stress and distortion predictions. The framework was then extended to model stress redistribution and gamma-prime precipitation during the pressing cycle. Gleeble tensile tests at varied heating rates support it.
doe-osti-3025050-subsurface-seismic-stru:
Luke Martin of the New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, with Martin Reyes, Adewale Amosu, and colleagues at New Mexico Tech. The team reports award DE-FE0032369, running December 2023 to November 2025 for the National Energy Technology Laboratory. The work characterizes the Hogback Monocline and the heat regime of the San Juan Basin in New Mexico, area of interest two. Such baselines matter where old oil and gas country is weighed for new subsurface uses.

Two data families anchor the study. Well logs give sharp, direct rock measurements at single boreholes, while seismic surveys cover the basin in three dimensions at lower resolution, tracing structure and rock boundaries. Chapters discuss joining the two, including machine learning pattern recognition for geophysical datasets where labeled training examples are scarce.
doe-osti-3025103-high-throughput-solvent:
Bryan Steinhoff of Navitas Advanced Solutions Group led award DE-EE0009109, from June 2020 to June 2024, with Arkema, Cabot, the University of Tennessee Knoxville, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory as partners. The goal was a solvent-free way to make lithium-ion battery electrodes at high throughput. Today's electrode lines coat slurries full of solvent that must then be dried off; the Advanced Dry Electrode Process skips that step.

Success turns on binder fibrillization, teasing the binder polymer into fine fibers that hold the electrode together without solvent. The team made free-standing cathodes near 6 and 12 milliamp-hours per square centimeter and a 6 milliamp-hour anode, then built half cells and tested formation and rate capability in duplicate. Both cathode cells showed little to no capacity fade over the reported cycling.
doe-osti-3365489-progressing-analysis-of:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's PAVER study, Progressing Analysis of Variable Electric Rates, dated March 2026, simulates what happens when utilities replace flat prices with rates that vary by time and system conditions. Hayden Reeve, Sadie Bender, Lane Smith, and six co-authors modeled several rate designs inside distribution system simulations, tracking bills for participants and non-participants separately. Fairness between the two groups is the design problem.

Two dynamic designs saved participating customers over 10 percent while holding non-participant bills within about 1 percent, rewarding flexibility without punishing neighbors. Some other simulated utilities saw non-participant bills rise up to 10 percent, a warning the authors flag. A subscription-style rate cut bill volatility by 17 percent but saved participants only 3.1 percent. Results give regulators evidence on which designs share gains broadly.
doe-osti-3367012-optimization-of-nb-sub-:
Old Dominion University's final report, by Hani E. Elsayed-Ali, optimizes sputter coating of niobium-tin superconductor onto accelerator cavities. Coating a cavity's inner surface with Nb3Sn lets it run efficiently at 4 kelvin instead of colder, cheaper helium temperatures, with high quality factors. The project used a direct-current cylindrical magnetron system fed by niobium and tin tube targets.

Process development ran on an aluminum mockup of a 2.6 gigahertz cavity, landing tin contents of 32 to 42 atomic percent at beam tube and equator positions. The best films came from annealing at 600 degrees Celsius for six hours, then 950 degrees for one hour. Applied to a real niobium cavity, the coating reached a transition temperature of 17.78 kelvin, near the best reported. A light tin recoating then improved radio frequency performance further.
doe-osti-3375016-advanced-manufacturing-:
A final report for Department of Energy award DE-EE0009107 covers a Sylvatex, Inc. project on cheaper ways to make lithium-ion cathode material. Virginia Klausmeier led the work, with Ahmed Al-Obeidi as co-author. The project ran from September 2020 to December 2025, with Argonne National Laboratory as a partner. The target product is NMC 622, a nickel-manganese-cobalt cathode mix used in electric vehicle cells.

The team refined a one-pot route that starts from metal acetates. Tables fix the recipe: feed rates, pH near eleven, and a stir rate of one thousand rpm. Calcination trials ran in a tube furnace at nine hundred degrees Celsius. Half coin cells were cycled at a C over three rate at thirty degrees. Their stability was compared head to head with a commercial powder. Plans called for fifty to one hundred grams to reach SpectraPower for pouch cell builds.
doe-osti-3394842-final-technical-report-:
Vedika Khemani of Stanford University closes Early Career award DE-SC0021111 with a final technical report titled The Non-Equilibrium Quantum Frontier. The award period ran from September 1, 2020 to August 31, 2025. The field is theoretical condensed matter physics under the Office of Basic Energy Sciences. The frontier is a regime science can now reach: many quantum particles, controlled and measured while staying coherent, far from equilibrium.

The program asked how the laws of statistical mechanics bend out of equilibrium. It studied how isolated quantum systems thermalize. It asked how thermalization can fail or run anomalously slow. It tracked how quantum information spreads or stays protected. And it mapped what new phases of matter appear in driven and measured systems. Information concepts, entanglement, learnability, scrambling, and error correction, supplied the diagnostics that organized the results.
doe-osti-3395395-development-of-in-situ-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4671, a CRADA document under agreement NFE-24-10231 dated March 2026, develops an in-situ polymerized, intrinsically conductive resin and low-cost carbon pigments. The team is Vipin Kumar, Subhabrata Saha, Sanjita Wasti, Yalcin Meraki of Oak Ridge and the University of Tennessee Knoxville, and Jesse Murphy. The targets named in the title are sensing, electromagnetic interference shielding, and lightning protection.

The abstract explains the opening. Conductive composites beat metals on weight, corrosion resistance, and processability. But plain polymers insulate. The usual fix, conductive fillers such as graphene, carbon nanotubes, MXene, or silver nanowire, is expensive. Its dispersion often breaks the conducting paths. Intrinsically conductive polymers exist, polyaniline chief among them, with high conductivity and stability. But they process poorly and are mechanically weak. The project set out to close exactly that gap.
doe-osti-3406847-tunable-two-dimensional:
Haiqing Lin of the State University of New York at Buffalo led a project on hollow fiber membranes for water recovery, under award DE-EE0009500. Partners included Helios-NRG, the National Energy Technology Laboratory, and Trimeric Corporation. The project ran from September 1, 2021 to July 31, 2025.

The fibers mix a polymer with thin, tunable two-dimensional porous material. Tests track how the membranes sort dyes and other matter from water. Life cycle checks weigh gains against chemical impacts. The goal is a membrane that cleans used water well and can be made at a useful scale for plants.
doe-osti-3409370-cfd-modeling-of-an-81-s:
Argonne report ANL-26/4, by M. Sitek, models drainage through a window in an 81-inch single slope barrier wall. Barrier walls line highways, and their drainage windows must pass gutter water safely. Both on-grade and sag road layouts were studied in detail.

Cutting the window height from 6 inches to 4 inches barely changed base-case results. Efficiency moved from 0.37 to 0.36 in that case. At a slope of 0.005 with a 10-foot spread, gutter depth reached 4.8 inches. Designers learn where window height matters and where slope and spread matter more. Designers can also compare on-grade and sag cases within the same run set.
doe-osti-3422383-potential-of-data-cente:
Pacific Northwest report, dated June 2026, asks how data center controls could sell services back to the grid. Alok Kumar Bharati, M. Al Mamun, Monish Mukherjee, and Frank K. Tuffner wrote the study. Data centers hold batteries, flexible loads, and fast controls that grids can use.

Battery reactive power support is modeled so it does not drain stored charge. Only active power moves change the battery state in the model. Most reactive support happens while power already flows in or out. That detail keeps service estimates honest. Grid operators can weigh data centers as helpers, not just burdens.
doe-osti-3589457-printable-low-cost-cata:
Lawrence Livermore report LLNL-TR-2020346 is the final report for a cooperative project on a printable low-cost catalyst. Swetha Chandrasekaran of Livermore is the named author, and Sigma-Aldrich was the industry partner. The agreement, CRADA TC02427, aimed to cut carbon output from industry. Its report date is April 5, 2026, within a three-year funding plan shared by the firm and the Energy Department.

The work centred on a direct ink writing ink made from graphene oxide and molybdenum disulfide. Such inks let printers build complex catalyst shapes with less waste than older methods. Goals were to make the ink in larger batches, keep its flow and thickness steady, and prove printed electrodes still worked well. User feedback drove repeat tweaks to the mix. The report closes with print protocols, stability checks, and steps toward wider use and sale.
doe-osti-3650938-accelerating-next-gener:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5T00-99639, dated August 2026, covers the BADGER project on faster cybersecurity work. Five authors are printed: Joshua Rivera, Abhijeet Sahu, Tim Coleman, Dana Hatic, and Alex Browning. BADGER stands for Broadband Automation for Distributed Grid Efficiency and Resilience. AI-driven attacks now move faster than defences built for human-led attacks, and wireless tools in the grid widen that gap.

The team compares three ways of building a cyber range. One is the classic human-led loop, bound by memory and slow manual search. A second adds GitHub Copilot as a coding helper inside the same loop. A third uses an agentic workflow that spans all phases of the build. A math framework scores each route on time, defects, risk, and cost. AI help enters as simple multipliers, keeping the model clear and easy to extend.
doe-osti-3827141-progress-on-additively-:
Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2026/4833, dated August 2026, advances the INFLUX fuel form, which swaps rods and pellets for woven lattice blocks. Fourteen team members from Oak Ridge and Idaho are named. In the lattice, fuel, cladding, and coolant thread through each other in smooth, repeating curves. No single printer can lay metal and ceramic together, so the team prints an empty lattice shell first. Ceramic beads fill the shell, and heat then seals the whole block shut.

For the water reactor line, laser printing of zirconium alloy reached wall density above ninety-nine percent. Zirconia beads were shaken into a one-port shell, a foil cap was laser-welded on, and hot pressing shrank the shell tight around the core. The graphite line fared worse: plastic templates broke under pressing or slumped when heated. The team dropped those routes and picked direct graphite printing instead.
doe-osti-3874835-evolution-of-r-matrix-p:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-28269, issued September 15, 2026, asks what happens when a nuclear scattering parameter is allowed to move. Joshua Adeleke is the sole printed author. In R-matrix theory, the channel radius is a free choice, and fits made at different radii are usually treated as unrelated. Adeleke instead promotes the radius to a flowing variable and tracks how resonance parameters drift. The write-up records a July 2026 workshop talk in Oak Ridge.

Differentiating the boundary matrix gives an exact evolution law of Riccati type; the scattering matrix stays radius-free exactly when that law holds. A closed form follows, with the physical phase shift as the constant of integration. Matching terms near each pole turns the flow into equations for pole energies and reduced widths. The width law carries an extra cubic term and a corrected invariant.
doe-osti-3931537-measurements-of-a-dorma:
Five Savannah River National Laboratory staff report how they measured smoke and weather during a dormant season prescribed burn at the Savannah River Site. They are Brianna Matthews, Brian Viner, Dalton Hare, Troy Lorier, and Stephen Noble. The report is dated September 2026. Land crews burn off growth in the cold months to cut wildfire risk. This team tracked what the fire put into the air.

Three portable weather stations ringed the burn plot. One stood upwind, and two stood where the smoke was expected to drift. A flux tower and drone flights added readings above the ground layer. Together the tools show how heat, wind, and smoke moved through the burn. Land managers can use the data to pick burn days when smoke stays thin over roads and homes.
doe-osti-3988984-influence-of-feedstock-:
Xinchang Zhang and Rongjie Song of Idaho National Laboratory, with Pavan Ajjarapu, Fred List, and Soumya Nag of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, ask how the starting powder shapes a pressed steel part. Their report, INL/RPT-26-95249, is dated August 2026. The steel is 316H, and the method is powder metallurgy with hot isostatic pressing.

The team pressed powder into solid billets, then cut samples for strength tests and close study of the grain structure. Chemical scans of an earlier billet from the same Sandvik powder batch found inclusion specks rich in manganese and oxygen, and larger ones rich in manganese, molybdenum, silicon, and oxygen. A heat treatment at 1150 degrees Celsius left the grain shape much the same. Powder quality, the report shows, leaves marks that no press cycle fully erases.
doe-osti-3991216-core-model-proposal-425:
Five Pacific Northwest National Laboratory staff — Katherine V. Calvin, Pralit L. Patel, Page Kyle, Patrick R. O'Rourke, and Anastasiia Zagoruichyk — log a round of bug fixes for the GCAM model in Core Model Proposal 425, report PNNL-39445, dated July 2026. GCAM is the lab's long-range model of energy, land, and climate links.

Each fix was checked three ways: the change was truly needed, the new inputs made sense, and the files ran clean. About fifty data chunks changed so a time-shift test could pass on version 8.6 of the model. The authors warn that core changes in version 9.0 will force more updates before the same test passes again. Extra test fixes ride along in the same proposal. Model maintainers get a clear record of what broke, what changed, and what still needs care.
dr-allinson-s-cookery-book-comprising-ma:
T. R. Allinson, a doctor who preached wholemeal bread and plain food, fills his 1915 cookery book with meat-free recipes. The index alone runs to hundreds of dishes, from almond cheesecakes and apple puddings to soups, batters, and blancmanges. A month's menu for one person and a week's menu show how the dishes fit a real table.

Recipes stay short and exact. A fruit and custard pudding, for one, takes stewed plums, a pint of milk, three eggs, breadcrumbs, sugar, and cinnamon. Apple cookery gets its own long run: cakes, charlottes, dumplings, fools, fritters, and dried apples. Allinson writes for health as much as taste, and his book served homes that kept a vegetarian table on a budget. It is a working kitchen book, not a showpiece, and its plain directions still read clearly.
furnishing-the-home-of-good-taste-a-brie:
Throop's Furnishing the Home of Good Taste surveys period styles in interior decoration and shows how to use them in modern homes. Lucy Abbot Throop begins with Egypt and Greece, then Italy's Renaissance and France's great reigns. Chapters follow Louis XIV, Louis XV, and Louis XVI, then the Empire style. English chapters run from Gothic days through Queen Anne, Chippendale, Robert Adam, Hepplewhite, and Sheraton. A revised edition appeared in 1920.

Later chapters treat Georgian furniture, French furniture, country houses, and the nursery. Curtains and floors get chapters of their own. Plates show paneling and cornices in real rooms. The book teaches taste as a learnable craft.
govdocs-archive_org-TridentineMassAlfons:
Alfons Cardinal Stickler, an Austrian cardinal and former prefect of the Vatican Library, gave this speech in the New York area in May 1995. His subject was the Tridentine Mass, the old Latin Mass, and why it continued to draw the faithful after its replacement.

Stickler argues that the new Mass produced by the post-conciliar liturgical commission betrayed what the fathers of Vatican II actually intended. He praises the old rite's reverence and its power to hold believers across centuries. The text preserves a senior churchman's case for the Latin Mass at a time when it was heavily restricted.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAOnassisArist:
Charles R. Babcock reported for the Washington Post on a claim by writer Jim Hougan. Hougan held that the CIA and Richard Nixon had approved, in 1954, a campaign of wiretapping and dirty tricks against Aristotle Onassis.

Onassis, the Greek shipping magnate, had cut an oil-tanker deal with Saudi Arabia that Washington wanted broken, and the reported campaign aimed at his empire. Hougan, an investigative writer on intelligence matters, brought the story out of old files two decades later. The article preserves the allegation as the Post presented it, a Cold War footnote with a billionaire at its center.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIReleases12-7:
An urgent FBI teletype left the Dallas office on November 26, 1963, four days after President Kennedy was shot in that city. The message reports information furnished by the governor's administrative assistant at Parkland Hospital. The governor, John Connally, lay wounded in that hospital, and his staff were witnesses to the day.

Teletypes were the Bureau's fastest paper, and the Dallas office used them around the clock that week. A message sourced to the governor's aide shows investigators gathering accounts from inside the hospital itself. The wire preserves the investigation at wire speed, before reports were polished.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GallenRichardPo: A letter dated November 3, 1994 was written to Raphaela Seroy about Richard Gallen. The writer, who is not identified in the text, discusses Gallen's personal difficulties. The letter also covers a dispute over retyping and editing Gallen's book manuscript, the kind of production quarrel that follows a difficult author and a troubled book toward print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewOrleansCouri:
Russell Ellwood wrote to Harold Weisberg on June 17, 1975, with a large claim. Ellwood said a Warren Commission transcript, obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, stated that Lee Harvey Oswald had worked as an FBI undercover agent. He asked for an interview with Weisberg and Jim Garrison for the New Orleans Courier.

Claims like Ellwood's arrived in Weisberg's mail often: a document half-read, a conclusion larger than the page. Weisberg usually answered such letters by asking for the document itself. The letter survives as evidence of the Courier's interest and of the rumors FOIA releases fed. It records what Ellwood believed the transcript said, which is not the same as what it said.
govdocs-archive_org-scottish-rite-bullet: The Scottish Rite Bulletin for January 1953 was issue No. 1 of that year's run from the Supreme Council of the fraternity. Among its items is a piece titled Upholding the Courts. Masonic bulletins carried news, speeches, and moral instruction to members across the country. The January issue shows the Rite speaking to its own in the early Cold War, in formal and patriotic tones.
govdocs-archive_org-the-runes-the-path-o: Juan Ricardo Céspedes studies the runes as more than an alphabet in The Runes and the Path of Initiation. The book covers the meanings of the runic signs and the history of the runes themselves. For Céspedes, each sign also marks a step on a path of inner training. The volume serves readers who approach runes as a spiritual system, not only as old letters carved in stone.
in-the-days-of-chivalry-a-tale-of-the-ti:
Evelyn Everett-Green set In the Days of Chivalry in the time of the Black Prince. Twin lads walk a Gascony forest in autumn as the tale opens. Leaves, wolves, and slanting sun fill the first pages. Raymond later recalls Father Paul and a solemn warning he had given.

An English summer visit stretches from October into August in one strand. The boys muse on whether prophetic fire dwelt in the priest. War, kinship, and faith in France and England shape the long tale. Everett-Green gives young readers a rich historical romance of knights and danger.
jahangir-tuzuk-i-jahangiri:
Jahangir, fourth Mughal emperor, wrote his own memoirs for the first nineteen years of his reign. The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, in Alexander Rogers's translation, covers 1605 onward in the emperor's frank voice. Few rulers of his age left so personal a record.

Jahangir writes of court plots, hunting trips, painting, wine, and justice. He pauses to note strange animals, fine mangoes, and the weights of fish he caught. His love of art and nature runs through the politics. The memoirs remain a prime source for Mughal India at its height. Court painters appear often, since Jahangir judged art with a keen, proud eye.
nasa-tm-19660012884-primordial-organic-c:
Opening pages of this work argue that the search for life beyond Earth is a central goal of space biology. A statement from the Space Science Board is quoted to that effect. The author ranks the question with the great shifts brought by Copernicus and by Darwin. If life on Mars were shown to have its own origin, he writes, the effect on thought would be immense.

The catalog note ties the work to the chemistry of early Earth, where life's building blocks first formed. Making biological molecules from simple gases is part of that story. The paper blends survey and argument. It captures the excitement of exobiology when Mars still seemed likely to hold life of its own.
nasa-tm-19680010317-ring-current-particl:
R. A. Hoffman and L. J. Cahill Jr., at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, issued this preprint in February 1968. It derives ring current particle distributions from ring current magnetic field measurements. The ring current is a vast loop of charged particles circling Earth, swelling during magnetic storms and distorting the planet's field.

Direct measurements of the current's particles were almost nonexistent: one satellite had only recently made the first such measurement. Field measurements, by contrast, existed, notably from the Explorer 26 magnetometer, which first displayed the current's location and its growth and decay through storms. Computing a field from a known particle distribution is straightforward, Hoffman notes, but running the problem backward is not. The paper takes on that harder inverse problem. It uses the particles' magnetic effects to infer their energy distribution.
nasa-tm-19710019759-terrestrial-environm:
Glenn E Daniels of the Marshall Space Flight Center edited this guideline book, issued May 10, 1971, as NASA TM X-64589. Daniels worked in the Aero Astrodynamics Laboratory. The book is the 1971 revision of NASA's terrestrial climate criteria. It tells space vehicle builders what weather their hardware must withstand on the ground. The catalog record stresses the Kennedy Space Center launch area.

Climate criteria cover wind, rain, heat, and cold at launch and storage sites. Designers use them to set strength and protection levels for vehicles and ground gear. A shared set of numbers keeps contractors and NASA centers consistent. Revisions like this one fold in newer weather records. The Kennedy emphasis reflects where most large launches then took place.
oregon-washington-and-alaska-sights-and-: Oregon, Washington and Alaska: Sights and Scenes for the Tourist is an 1890 railroad guidebook. Its author, E. L. Lomax, was general passenger agent of the Union Pacific System. The book was published from Omaha to draw travelers onto the line's routes west. The hosted sample shows only the front matter. Illustrated title pages carry the compliments of the Union Pacific passenger department. A list of the company's ticket agents follows. The sightseeing text itself does not appear, so this note claims nothing about its descriptions.
phelim-otoole-s-courtship-and-other-stor:
William Carleton's Phelim O'Toole's Courtship leads this volume of his Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry. Phelim, an only son, is heir to a snug estate of half an acre. His grandfather won it from the English, as the story goes, at the point of his reaping-hook, and took it at a moderate rent paid in daily labour.

Carleton first sets out the sorrow of Phelim's parents, seven years married without a child, in a cottage of unbearable stillness. The volume adds Wildgoose Lodge, Tubber Derg, Neal Malone, and Art Maguire. Carleton wrote the Irish peasantry from inside, with comedy laid over hardship.
podcast-tuckercarlson-59hVEPze1rI:
Economist Oren Cass talks with Tucker Carlson about tariffs and trade. Cass leads a policy group that favors making more goods inside the United States. He supports the tariff push tied to Donald Trump.

Cass says the old trade system served foreign policy more than American workers. He argues it held together a global order while factories left home. He urges firms to plan now for higher import costs. The talk lays out a calm, detailed case for a reset in how America trades with the world. He warns that a sudden shift would still bring real pain first.
the-annals-of-the-parish-or-the-chronicl:
John Galt arranged and edited this parish chronicle, shown in a 1910 London and Edinburgh edition from T. N. Foulis with color pictures by Henry W. Kerr. The writer in the book is the Reverend Micah Balwhidder, who tells the story of his own ministry at Dalmailing in Scotland.

Balwhidder begins with a pleasing match of dates. In the same year, on the same day of the same month, that King George the Third came to his crown, Balwhidder was settled as minister of the parish. Neighbors marveled at the pairing and read the hand of providence in it. He and the king, they said, were bound to fade and flourish together, and so, he hints, it proved.
the-best-short-stories-of-1921-and-the-y: Edward J. O'Brien edited an annual of best short stories for 1921, paired with a yearbook of the American short story, published in Boston by Small, Maynard and Company. O'Brien is listed as editor of similar annuals from 1915 through 1920. The opening pages are copyright notices, naming many publishers and authors whose work is reprinted, among them Harper and Brothers, Scribner's, Fannie Hurst, and Susan Glaspell. No story text, contents list, or introduction appears in these pages.
the-cross-and-the-shamrock-or-how-to-def: The Cross and the Shamrock, or How to Defend the Faith, calls itself an Irish-American Catholic tale of real life, printed in Boston by Patrick Donahoe of Franklin Street. Its title page promises an account of the temptations, sufferings, trials, and triumphs of the children of St. Patrick in the great republic of Washington, offered for the amusement and special instruction of Catholic male and female servants in the United States. The title page credits the writing to a missionary priest, and only that title page is present here.
the-every-day-life-of-abraham-lincoln-a-:
The Every-Day Life of Abraham Lincoln heads its pages with verse by Lowell. He calls Lincoln a shepherd of mankind. The man loved his charge, the verse says, but never loved to lead. Folk joyed to be led by him. They prized his clear-grained human worth. They prized his brave old wisdom too.

A second verse turns to fame. Great captains stir us for an hour with guns and drums. Then silence comes, and they are gone. Our children, it says, shall see Lincoln's fame stand like a tower. The book then gathers tales of his daily rounds. Law office, store, and White House all supply their share.
the-hand-but-not-the-heart-or-the-life-t:
T. S. Arthur wrote The Hand but Not the Heart; or, The Life-Trials of Jessie Loring, published in New York in 1858. Chapter one opens at a social gathering where Mrs. Denison finds a young man, Paul Hendrickson, standing still and lost in thought. She teases him for looking more like a statue than a living man.

Paul tries to brush the remark aside, yet his manner shows he does not feel the calm he claims. He insists he has stood there only a few minutes, while Mrs. Denison puts the time at twenty minutes or more. Their light exchange sets up a story, named in the title, about love given in form but not in feeling.
the-last-american-a-fragment-from-the-jo:
J. A. Mitchell presented his 1889 satire as the journal of Khan-Li, a Persian prince and admiral. Persian scholars of a later age study the Mehrikans, a people said to have vanished as a nation by 1990. A museum curator at Shiraz supplies praise and reading advice in an opening note.

Mitchell flips the travel book form on its head. Future Persians tour ruined America and puzzle over its shallow, nervous, and extravagant habits, as the curator puts the charge. American readers of 1889 were meant to see their own country through mocking foreign eyes.
the-lock-and-key-library-classic-mystery:
Julian Hawthorne edited The Lock and Key Library volume of Classic Mystery and Detective Stories devoted to modern English writers, issued in New York by the Review of Reviews Company in 1909. The title page names its stars: Rudyard Kipling, A. Conan Doyle, Egerton Castle, Stanley J. Weyman, Wilkie Collins, and Robert Louis Stevenson. The volume opens with Kipling's My Own True Ghost Story.

Kipling starts with a joke about Walter Besant, a writer of real stories about real people who insists on treating his ghosts seriously. A frontispiece by Power O'Malley, drawn for Kipling's In the House of Suddhoo, shows a jet of fire sent from a man's nostrils. Readers get a shelf of famous names mixing detective work, mystery, and the supernatural.
travels-of-richard-and-john-lander-into-:
Robert Huish compiled the travels of Richard and John Lander from unpublished papers held by the late Captain John William Barber Fullerton. The London edition of 1836 sets one goal in its title: tracing the course and end of the Niger. A long introduction surveys earlier African exploration.

Huish opens with a prefatory analysis of Park, Denham, Clapperton, Adams, Lyon, Ritchie, and others. His introduction argues that discovery often owed more to chance than to design, with America as the grand example. The Landers' own journeys then follow, built from documents of the African service. Readers gain both the expedition record and a survey of what came before it.
wild-beasts-and-their-ways-reminiscences: Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, so Samuel W. Baker's hunting tales do not appear. The header names the book Wild Beasts and Their Ways, by Sir Samuel W. Baker. It is number 7 in a Gutenberg series of Baker's works. Release is dated January 2003, as etext number 3657. The first posting date is July 3, 2001, and the edition is number 10. The rest is standard header text on copyright, donations, and the archive foundation.
